article_content: Wayne Rooney has revealed that the inspiration behind his cartwheel goal celebration during Englandâs 3-1 win against Scotland was his five-year-old son, Kai. In an Instagram post on Friday, the former Manchester United striker explained that Kai had asked him to perform the acrobatic move if he scored at Celtic Park. Rooney shared a 14-second video of Kai doing cartwheels in the Wembley tunnel before Englandâs 3-1 victory over Slovenia on Saturday. In the clip, Kai is wearing a full England kit with 'Daddy 100' on the back and appears delighted after completing the maneuver. Rooney was once banned by Sir Alex Ferguson from celebrating goals with a cartwheel at Manchester United, following an incident in January 2010 after he scored the winning goal in a Carling Cup semi-final second leg against Manchester City â a move deemed too risky. Although Rooney celebrated his first goal against Scotland in a traditional manner, he honored his sonâs request after scoring his second goal late in the match, executing a perfect cartwheel. In his Instagram caption, Rooney wrote: 'Lots of people are asking why I did a cartwheel to celebrate my goal against Scotland. Itâs because my son Kai has been doing them a lot lately and asked me to do one. Here he is doing one in the tunnel before the @england vs Slovenia game!' The video shows Kai and his younger brother, Klay, preparing to join their father on the pitch at Wembley. Rooney scored twice in the 3-1 win over Scotland at Celtic Park on Tuesday, bringing his international tally to 46 goals â surpassing Jimmy Greaves and moving within three of Sir Bobby Charltonâs record of 49. Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain opened the scoring for England with a fine header after 32 minutes, assisted by Jack Wilshere. Rooney extended the lead shortly after halftime, and Andrew Robertson of Hull City pulled one back for Scotland seven minutes before full time. Rooney sealed the victory with his second goal in the 85th minute, capping off a slick team move. Rooney recently received a special golden cap from Sir Bobby Charlton in recognition of his 100 international appearances. He marked the occasion by scoring a penalty, then added these two goals against Scotland.

article_content: Real Madrid are reportedly preparing a staggering Â£76 million offer to lure Luis Suarez away from Liverpoolâa move that could ignite one of the most dramatic transfer sagas of the summer. While Liverpool have already sealed the signing of Emre Can and are openly stating Suarez is not for sale, the Uruguayan forwardâs future remains uncertain. Suarez himself insists heâs happy at Anfield and believes the club is heading in the right direction, but even those close to him admit they canât predict how heâll respond if Madrid keep raising their offer. Last year, Liverpool famously resisted Arsenalâs advances for Suarez, with then-manager Brendan Rodgers pulling off a managerial masterstroke that earned the strikerâs heartfelt gratitude. But Real Madrid arenât Arsenalâtheyâre a global powerhouse with Cristiano Ronaldo and Gareth Bale waiting in the wings, plus the financial muscle to make any deal real. Add in potential trade-ins like Fabio Coentrao and Alvaro Morata, and the temptation grows. Liverpoolâs counterargumentâthat Suarez would remain their undisputed starâis strong, but the allure of Madridâs stage might be too potent to ignore. Elsewhere, Thomas Muller could be heading for a reunion with Louis van Gaal at Manchester United. Though United officially deny interest, reports suggest an approach was made, and with Hernandez and Welbeck possibly leaving, scouting Mullerâs availability makes senseâeven if midfield and defense remain top priorities. At Blackburn, Jordan Rhodes is effectively off the market unless a Â£15 million bid lands on the tableâand even then, the clubâs 25% sell-on clause means they wonât let him go lightly. Meanwhile, Norwich City may miss out, while QPR and Crystal Palace eye Gary Hooper. Feyenoord are circling Ricky van Wolfswinkel, and Newcastle continue their hunt for strikers, with free agent Bafetimbi Gomis holding out for Â£100,000 a weekâa figure that narrows his options drastically. On the youth front, Crystal Palaceâs 20-year-old Jonny Williams caught the eye against Holland, drawing attention from Swansea, Hull, and Southampton. Manchester Cityâs Emyr Huws also impressed in his brief appearance. But the biggest buzz surrounds 17-year-old Anderlecht midfielder Youri Tielemansâalready the youngest Belgian to feature in the Champions Leagueâwith Chelsea, Man City, Spurs, Arsenal, Roma, and Juventus all keeping tabs. Similarly, 20-year-old Argentine striker Luciano Vietto, who holds an Italian passport and wants to join a Premier League side under Gus Poyet, is being tracked by Liverpool, Everton, and Sunderland, with a Â£6 million price tag attached. Sheffield United have moved quickly to sign free agent Chris Basham, whoâs undergoing a medical, while also pursuing Halifax striker Lee Gregory amid competition from Millwall. article_content: Ross Lawson, 32, was sentenced to two years in prison for operating a high-end brothel disguised as the Steam and Sun Health Club, a five-star massage parlour in Camden, North London. For seven years, the business operated 18 hours a day and generated more than Â£1 million annually, with dozens of sex workers earning up to Â£100,000 per year. Lawson collected Â£75,000 each Friday night and used the profits to pay off Â£8,000 monthly credit card bills and fund a luxurious lifestyle for himself and his family. Despite its illicit nature, the operation maintained legal appearances: Lawson obtained proper licenses from Camden Council, filed tax returns, and registered employees for National Insurance. The establishment offered sauna and steam rooms, an upscale bar, and VIP suites, advertising itself as Londonâs only five-star massage parlour. During a February 2012 police raid, officers found 27 sex workers, patrons engaged in sexual activity, and Â£3,000 in cash. Internal communications revealed Lawson instructed staff to provide 'a complete service' to all clients, regardless of appearance. At Blackfriars Crown Court, a jury convicted Lawson of running a brothel and three counts of money laundering. Judge Peter Murphy described the operation as 'remarkably successful' and 'well organized,' noting that its profitability stemmed almost entirely from Lawsonâs management. However, the judge commended the working conditions, stating Lawson did not exploit the women, and reduced the sentence accordingly. Lawsonâs sister, Jade, 27, a law graduate from the University of Hertfordshire, worked as the receptionist. She was acquitted of managing the brothel but convicted of money laundering after accepting Â£30,000 from her brother to settle her student loans. The judge called her involvement an 'aberration' unlikely to be repeated, sentencing her to a suspended six-month jail term and a curfew. Barman Waldemar Walczak, 29, was convicted of profiting from the brothel and transferring Â£53,000 to his wife and brother-in-law. His relatives, Karolina and Rafal Ginter, were acquitted of possessing criminal property. Walczakâs sentencing is scheduled for August 19.

Recent violence in Iraq has intensified challenges for Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki and his government, raising doubts about his capacity to maintain national unity amid a resurgent insurgency. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry stated on Sunday that the United States will support Iraqâs efforts against al Qaeda-linked militants in western Iraqâbut emphasized that no U.S. troops will be deployed. As instability grows, here are five critical questions about the crisis:

1. I thought the Iraq War was over. Why is there still fighting?
Actually, last year was the deadliest since 2008. Fatalities reached levels not seen since the peak of the Iraq War, when sectarian conflict between the Shia majority and Sunni minority nearly plunged the country into civil war. Tensions persist due to widespread Sunni grievances: many feel politically marginalized and targeted by aggressive security measures. Al-Maliki has instructed troops to avoid striking neighborhoods in Falluja, yet protests have been forcibly dispersed in both Falluja and Ramadiâsparking renewed unrest. Some Sunni military officers have defected to join insurgent groups, attacking police stations and prisons. With national elections approaching in April, fears are growing that violence could spiral into full-scale civil conflict.

2. I thought al Qaeda was on the run. Now do they control parts of Iraq?
While the U.S. successfully weakened al Qaedaâs core leadership in Afghanistan and Pakistan, its regional affiliatesâincluding ISIS (Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham)âhave gained strength since the 2011 U.S. troop withdrawal. Exploiting sectarian divisions and weak governance, ISIS has launched deadly attacks on government institutions, killing thousands. Recent reports indicate ISIS has seized control of large parts of Falluja and much of Ramadi. Iraqi forces are now engaged in fierce battles to retake these cities.

3. Falluja and Ramadi were crucial during the Iraq War. Wonât the U.S. help?
Yesâboth cities were pivotal battlegrounds. In 2004, U.S. Marines fought one of their bloodiest battles in Falluja to oust insurgents. In Ramadi, the U.S.-backed 'Awakening' movement rallied Sunni tribes against al Qaeda, turning the tide of the war. But with U.S. troops fully withdrawn, Washington is unwilling to return. Kerry reiterated: âThis is their fight.â The U.S. will provide air support, intelligence, and weaponsâbut no boots on the ground.

4. What does Syria have to do with it?
The Syrian civil war has directly fueled Iraqâs instability. ISIS, originally al Qaeda in Iraq, rebranded itself to reflect its ambitions in Syria and Lebanon. It seeks to establish a transnational Islamic caliphate governed by sharia law. Anbar Province shares a 400-mile border with Syria, allowing militants to move freely and launch cross-border attacks. With recent losses in Syria, ISIS has shifted focus toward consolidating power in Iraq.

5. Are ISIS fighters also active in Lebanon?
Unfortunately, yes. ISIS claimed responsibility for a suicide bombing in a Hezbollah-controlled neighborhood of Beirut and threatened further attacks if Hezbollah continues supporting Assadâs regime in Syria. The weakening of state institutions in Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon has created fertile ground for extremist groups. Experts warn that the conflict is increasingly becoming a proxy war between Shia Iran and Sunni Saudi Arabia. A full-blown Iraqi civil war, alongside Syriaâs, could trigger broader regional chaos. Despite U.S. efforts, al Qaedaâs legacyânow embodied by ISISâis not only alive but growing.

When father-of-two Kamal Hussain received a letter from his childrenâs school stating that classes would end early for staff development, he arranged for his kids to have the afternoon off. But he grew suspicious when he saw three teachers in smart clothing driving past himâdespite being scheduled to remain at school for the INSET (in-service training) afternoon. Visiting the empty school, he was told by a cleaner that the headteacher and staff had left for a colleagueâs wedding. Furious, Mr. Hussain drove to the venue and confronted Headteacher Gillian Pursey, whom he found seated with around 23 staff members at the reception. Mr. Hussain condemned the school for sending what he called a 'blatant lie' in an official notice to parents. 'I teach my children not to lieâwhat kind of example is this?' he said. 'Iâve lost my trust in them and am considering moving my children elsewhere.' He also demanded an investigation, arguing that students had collectively lost hundreds of hours of instruction. article_content: Scientists have discovered vast reservoirs of water buried deep within Earthâs crustâsome as old as 2.7 billion years. These ancient fluids, trapped in fractures of Precambrian rocks across Canada, South Africa, and Scandinavia, may host entirely new forms of microbial life. Researchers estimate the total volume exceeds 2.5 million cubic miles, surpassing all rivers, lakes, and wetlands on the planet combined. The water is not just oldâitâs chemically extreme. Reacting with surrounding rock, it generates significant amounts of hydrogen, mimicking processes seen at deep-sea hydrothermal vents. This chemistry creates a highly saline, viscous fluidâso thick it resembles light maple syrupâand turns orange upon exposure to air due to oxidized iron minerals. Professor Barbara Sherwood Lollar from the University of Toronto, who led the research, admits she tasted it: 'Itâs terrible,' she said. 'Much saltier than seawater. You wouldnât want to drink it.' But its chemical makeup offers clues to how life might survive in extreme environmentsâeven on Mars, whose ancient crust may behave similarly. Using noble gas isotopes, scientists dated the water to over a billion years in some locations, with pockets possibly as old as the rocks themselves. These findings, published in Nature and presented at the American Geophysical Union, reveal that hydrogen production in Earthâs continental crust is far higher than previously assumedâroughly equal to that of the ocean floor. This dramatically reshapes our view of Earthâs deep biosphere. If microbes can thrive in such conditions here, similar ecosystems might exist underground on Mars. Meanwhile, separate research from Ohio State University suggests Earthâs surface water may have originated not only from icy comets but also from water slowly squeezed out of minerals in the mantle over billions of yearsâvia plate tectonics. Minerals like ringwoodite and garnet appear capable of storing and releasing hydrogen and oxygen, potentially fueling our planetâs water cycle on a geological timescale. The implications? Earthâs hidden water systems could be central to its habitabilityânot just as a resource, but as a driver of planetary evolution.

article_content: Boyd Gaines, 59, and Kathleen McNenny, 50, met 20 years ago and are appearing together as a couple in Broadwayâs new production of An Enemy of the People. The updated version of Henrik Ibsenâs play opens September 27 and centers on a married couple who have been together for two decades. Few people will accuse Boyd Gaines and Kathleen McNenny of lacking onstage chemistry. The actors, who met two decades ago, married, and raised a child together, are sharing the stage as a couple for the first time â a rare case of art imitating life. 'The play is about a marriage that is at least 20 years old. Itâs about a marriage that has children,' said McNenny, 50, reflecting on the instant intimacy their real-life bond brings to the role. 'If we came in with people we didnât know, there would be a period of time before you could build trust. With us, a lot of steps got cut out.' New York theatergoers will see the husband-and-wife duo up close as they star in the Manhattan Theatre Clubâs production of An Enemy of the People, a contemporary adaptation of Henrik Ibsenâs classic. Gaines plays a public-spirited doctor in a small town who uncovers that the water supply at the local spa is contaminated â potentially making tourists, the townâs economic lifeline, sick. His attempts to expose the truth pit his ethics against political cowardice and media indifference, and his family suffers â including his wife, portrayed by McNenny. During a joint interview, McNenny said: 'You always want to work with people who are better than you. Not only do I get to work with someone who is truly exceptional onstage, but I also feel safe. I donât feel intimidated â because itâs my husband.' Her four-time Tony Award-winning husband, Gaines, disagrees: 'Iâm certainly not better than she is. God knows thatâs not true. Iâm always dumbstruck by how creative Kathy is and how much she brings to the table.' Fitting for two actors, Gaines and McNenny first fell for each other onstage. They were cast as Luciana and Antipholus of Ephesus in the 1992 Public Theater production of William Shakespeareâs The Comedy of Errors in Central Park. Though theyâd briefly met while filming the 1991 miniseries A Woman Named Jackie, it was director Cace Rosset who formally introduced them during private casting meetings. Gaines had just left Rossetâs office when McNenny arrived for her turn. Rosset reintroduced them and asked, 'So, do you think you can fall in love?' 'We both shrugged and said, 'Well, sure â thatâs our job. Weâre actors; weâre supposed to act that,''' Gaines recalled. McNenny added: 'I said, 'Sure, Iâll fall in love with him. Fine.'' After the show ended, they began dating. Over the years, theyâve shared the stage only rarely: a two-night benefit on Broadway in 2002, a production at the Westport Country Playhouse in 2003, and A.R. Gurneyâs Sylvia at the George Street Playhouse in New Brunswick, New Jersey, in 2010 â until now. Why so few joint roles? 'First of all, Boyd can do musicals and I canât,' said McNenny. 'Well, they let me do them occasionally,' Gaines replied modestly. 'I donât know if I can â certainly not well.'

article_content: Mastercard has come under scrutiny for collecting and selling anonymized transaction data to advertisers. Through its MasterCard Advisors Media Solutions Group, the company claims it can identify high-spending consumer segments and help advertisers target them effectively. While Mastercard asserts that no personally identifiable information â such as names or addresses â is ever collected or shared, it refuses to disclose how its data aggregation system works. According to Susan Grossman, Senior Vice President at MasterCard Advisors Media Solutions Group, the foundation of the service is transaction data: date, time, amount, and merchant information gathered when consumers swipe their cards. Billions of anonymous transactions are aggregated into behavioral segments â such as frequent restaurant goers or holiday shoppers â and sold to advertisers as targeted audiences. An internal presentation titled 'Leveraging MasterCard Data Insights to Reach Holiday Shoppers' promotes the service to potential clients, highlighting the ability to predict peak spending periods. Mastercard confirms the program runs exclusively in the United States and relies on data from 1.8 billion payment cards. Privacy advocates, including Big Brother Watch, have criticized the initiative, arguing that consumers are not informed or given meaningful opportunities to opt out. Nick Pickles, Director of Big Brother Watch, stated: 'If this data has value, it should be up to Mastercard to ask customers for permission â and offer something in return. Instead, they're treating personal behavior as their own property to be bundled and sold.' Mastercard maintains that its practices comply with privacy standards, emphasizing that all data is aggregated and anonymized, and that protecting consumer trust is 'core' to its values.

article_content: The striking parallels between Justin Rose and Adam Scott â born just two weeks apart â have now extended beyond their careers and into their personal lives. Both elite golfers now call the same island in the Bahamas home, mere steps away from each other. As Rose climbs into contention at The Open, his wife Kate has been finalizing their move from Orlando, settling into a residence near Scott and his new wife. The duo now share private jets to tournaments and often walk the fairways together, united by ambition and camaraderie. Their goal: to make the next five years a defining era, leaving a legacy as enduring as those of Sir Nick Faldo and Greg Norman. Scott, currently World No. 1, has long been the trailblazer â reaching every major milestone just ahead of Rose, who is slightly younger. Both have won PGA Tour, European Tour, and World Golf Championship events, plus a major each: Scott took the Masters in 2013; Rose claimed the U.S. Open the same year. At The Open, Scott sits at three-under after a 73, one stroke ahead of Roseâs two-under 70. With Rory McIlroy leading at 12-under, the race remains wide open. Despite challenging conditions, both delivered resilient rounds. Scottâs putting has been inconsistent â he created numerous birdie chances but failed to convert many, often reacting with frustration. Rose, meanwhile, didnât sink a single putt on Friday but still stayed in contention thanks to clutch chip-ins and an eagle on the 10th. As Graeme McDowell noted, the future of their rivalry hinges on putting. Once the long putter ban takes effect in 2016, Scottâs advantage may wane. McDowell predicts a close battle: perhaps four majors for Scott, three for Rose â or vice versa. Their shared journey â from birthdates to bunkers â feels almost scripted. Yet their drive, precision, and quiet determination suggest this is no coincidence. The next chapter may be written not just on the leaderboard, but in the quiet moments between friends who are also rivals.

article_content: FIFA has identified two potential winter dates for the 2022 World Cup in Qatar: January/February 2022 or November/December 2022. Both options would significantly disrupt the traditional global football calendar. While clubs have urged FIFA to consider May 2022, concerns over extreme heat during that period remain a major obstacle. FIFA Secretary General Jerome Valcke confirmed that discussions are narrowing toward one of the two winter windows. He stated, 'We are getting closer to finalizing the dates â either January/February or November/December 2022 â but weâve also received input regarding May 2022. Weâll summarize feedback and provide updates ahead of the next meeting.' Qatar 2022 CEO Hassan Al Thawadi echoed that winter is the 'ideal situation' for the Middle East, though the traditional June/July timeframe remains under consideration. FIFA President Sepp Blatter awarded the tournament to Qatar in 2010. An artistâs rendering of the proposed Al-Khor Stadium has also been shared as part of the ongoing preparations.

article_content: After being hacked and briefly taken offline, the official website of Ohioâs Secretary of State, Jennifer Brunner, has been restored. Brunner confirmed that while her office faced cyberattacks and a wave of threatening communicationsâincluding death threats and a suspicious envelope marked 'Death to Obama supporters'âno sensitive data was compromised. She credited her staff for remaining resilient amid the pressure, noting that these incidents are not isolated but part of a broader pattern of harassment targeting her office, often originating from outside Ohio. The Ohio Highway Patrol is now investigating the cyber intrusion, the threats, and the mysterious package sent to a former office location. These events coincide with an ongoing legal battle between Brunnerâs office and the state Republican Party, which has accused her of failing to properly verify voter registrations ahead of the 2008 election. The U.S. Supreme Court recently intervened, blocking a lower courtâs directive that would have forced Brunner to update voter rolls after discrepancies emerged between new registrations and federal databases. While Republicans claim this undermines election integrity, experts like the Brennan Center for Justice stress that actual voter fraud is exceedingly rare. Most reported irregularities stem from third-party registrars submitting fake formsânot from individuals voting illegally. Critics argue such disputes are being used to justify efforts that could suppress turnout among Democratic-leaning voters, echoing controversies from the 2004 election, when similar allegations were made but never substantiated by federal investigators.

article_content: American Sniper has shattered box office records, earning more than $110 million in its first four weeks. However, this unprecedented success may impact the murder trial of Eddie Ray Routh, the man accused of killing Chris Kyle, according to attorneys involved in the case. Former Marine Eddie Ray Routh is set to go to trial on February 11 â two years after he allegedly shot and killed Kyle and Kyleâs friend, Chad Littlefield, at a Texas firing range. At the time, Kyle was attempting to help Routh manage his post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Routh has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Although American Sniper does not depict the shooting itself â the film ends with footage of Kyleâs funeral â Routhâs defense team argues that the filmâs massive popularity, media attention, and Oscar nominations could compromise jury impartiality. 'The film will be an issue,' said Routhâs attorney, J. Warren St. John, in an interview with People magazine. 'Any case with significant publicity faces challenges in selecting an impartial jury. Iâve handled cases like this before. National attention makes it extremely difficult.' Jurors are expected to be unbiased and uninformed about the case prior to trial. In 2013, a judge imposed a gag order to limit media commentary from those involved in the case, anticipating widespread public interest. Routhâs lawyers also unsuccessfully sought to move the trial outside Texas, where public sentiment toward Kyle remains intensely favorable. American Sniper recently won the Academy Award for Best Picture. Its debut weekend grossed a record-breaking $107 million in North America â the highest January opening ever. The film, directed by Clint Eastwood and starring Bradley Cooper, has been nominated for six Oscars, including Best Picture and Best Actor. The movie has ignited fierce public debate. Documentary filmmaker Michael Moore criticized it for glorifying Kyle, while former Alaska governor Sarah Palin condemned critics, writing on Facebook: 'Leftists are not fit to shine Chris Kyleâs combat boots.' She added: 'God bless our troops, especially our snipers.' 'Mr. Kyle is a hero in many peopleâs eyes,' said George Parnham, a Houston-based criminal defense attorney unaffiliated with the case. 'Given the intense public attention this film has received, itâs doubtful a truly fair jury can be seated anywhere.' On February 2, 2013, Routh, then 26, fatally shot Kyle, 38, and Littlefield, 35, near Chalk Mountain, Texas. Kyle had invited Routh to the range as part of an effort to help him recover from PTSD. American Sniper is based on Kyleâs bestselling autobiography of the same name.

Justice Secretary Kenny MacAskill announced the change, stating it would bring Scotland in line with most European nations while establishing a stricter standard than England and Wales. MacAskill emphasized that the move sends a clear message: there is no excuse for drinking and driving. 'Drink-driving shatters families and communities,' he said. 'Every year, around 20 families lose a loved one, and roughly 760 people are treated for injuries caused by drivers who chose to drink and get behind the wheel. We cannot let this continue.' He cited research showing that even one drink can triple the risk of a fatal crash, and that approximately one in ten road deaths in Scotland involves a driver over the legal limit. The proposed legislation, which received parliamentary approval, aimed to save lives and make roads safer. The Scottish Governmentâs decision followed a public consultation in which nearly 75% of respondents supported lowering the limit. MacAskill added: 'If youâve had any alcohol, donât drive. Full stop. Taking responsibility means protecting lives.' The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) welcomed the move, urging the rest of the UK to adopt similar measures. Sandy Allan, RoSPAâs Road Safety Manager in Scotland, noted: 'Research consistently shows that lowering drink-drive limits reduces deaths and injuries. Scotlandâs leadership here must inspire the rest of the UK.'

article_content: A Costco employee allegedly kicked and broke a customerâs leg at the storeâs exit, according to a lawsuit filed by Timothy Walls. The Oregonian reports that Walls, in his $670,000 lawsuit, claims two Portland-area Costco employees were involved in the incident. Walls alleges that after he failed to show his receipt â which documented a $103 purchase â one employee yanked his shopping cart. He then reportedly grabbed the employee by the shirt collar, leading to what he describes as a 'martial arts-style strike' from a second employee, The Oregonian reported. Costcoâs official policy states: 'To ensure that all members are correctly charged for the merchandise purchased, all receipts and merchandise will be inspected as you leave the warehouse.' Disagreements persist over whether the altercation occurred inside the warehouse or outside near the exit. Walls contends it happened outside; Costco maintains it occurred within the store. Wallsâ attorney, Clayton Morrison, argued that the core legal question is: 'What can Costco lawfully do? Can they actually stop you and take your property?' His position is: 'No.' In a court filing obtained by The Oregonian, Costcoâs attorney, Bill Stockton, asserted that Wallsâ own conduct, fault, and negligence led to his injuries. Requests for comment sent to both attorneys by MailOnline were not immediately answered.

article_content: Cairo (CNN) â Egyptian authorities said Sunday they are preparing for a new round of negotiations with Germy Abu Masouh, a Bedouin tribesman who kidnapped two American tourists and an Egyptian tour guide, demanding the release of his uncle from an Alexandria jail. General Ahmed Bakr, head of security in Egyptâs northern Sinai Peninsula, said Bedouin sheikhs acting as mediators have confirmed the hostages â Michel Louis, a pastor at Bostonâs Free Pentecostal Church of God; Lisa Alphonse, a parishioner; and an Egyptian tour guide â are unharmed and well-fed. Authorities identify Abu Masouh as a member of a prominent Sinai Bedouin tribe. His uncle, according to Bakr, was arrested in Alexandria with approximately half a ton of drugs. Negotiations involve senior intelligence and police officials. 'We hope to reach a resolution soon,' Bakr said. 'Abu Masouh has threatened to kidnap more tourists if his demands are not met.' Abu Masouh told Egyptian media that Louis had been permitted to call his wife, who was on the same bus. However, Daniel Louis, the pastorâs son, disputed this claim Sunday afternoon: 'We spoke to my mother. She said she has not spoken to my father.' Michel Louis, who has diabetes, may not have access to his medication, his son added. Jean Louis, another son, told CNNâs 'Early Start Weekend' that the group was traveling toward Israel when their bus was stopped by armed men in vehicles near the Sinai Peninsula. The family, unaware of security risks in the region, expressed faith in Godâs protection. 'If we had known the dangers, we would have made a different decision,' Jean Louis said. Bakr placed partial blame on the travel agency for failing to notify authorities of the itinerary. 'If they had, we would have provided a police escort,' he said. Authorities confirm the hostages remain in the area where they were taken. Kidnappings and armed robberies have risen since the 2011 ouster of President Hosni Mubarak. The U.S. Embassy in Cairo stated on Twitter Friday that it is 'in close touch with Egyptian authorities, who are doing everything they can to bring about the safe release of the American tourists.' CNNâs Mohamed Fadel Fahmy reported from Cairo; Saad Abedine from Atlanta. Richard Allen Greene and Randi Kaye contributed to this report.

article_content: A German broadcaster has canceled reruns of the detective series 'Derrick' after it was revealed that its late star, Horst Tappert, had served in Hitler's Waffen-SS. Tappert, who portrayed the iconic detective in the long-running show, concealed his military past until his death in 2008. Archives uncovered last month that he had served in the Totenkopf panzer division â one of the most notorious units of the Waffen-SS, the armed wing of the Nazi paramilitary organization. ZDF, Germanyâs public broadcaster, stated it was 'shocked and troubled' by the revelation. A spokesperson told AFP: 'We have no plans to broadcast any more reruns. We will not honor an actor who lied about his past.' According to historical records, Tappert was a 19-year-old panzer grenadier when he was wounded on the Eastern Front in 1943. He previously claimed he had served only as a medic. The Totenkopf division, whose motto was 'My Honour is Loyalty,' was responsible for numerous war crimes and became one of the most feared units of the Waffen-SS. Bavariaâs interior ministry is now considering revoking the honorary title of chief police inspector awarded to Tappert in 1980, according to BBC reports citing German media. Between 1974 and 1998, more than 280 episodes of 'Derrick' were produced. Set in Munich and starring the distinctive, bespectacled detective, the series was immensely popular across Germany and internationally, including in Russia, China, and South Africa. The controversy echoes a similar outcry in 2006 when renowned German author GÃ¼nter Grass disclosed his own brief service in the Waffen-SS.

article_content: At just 11 years old, Ava May Llewellyn has made history by becoming the first martial arts black belt to earn a place at the Royal Ballet School â a feat that blends discipline, grace, and sheer determination. Born and raised in Downend, Bristol, Ava began dancing before she could walk properly and took up Taekwondo at age four after watching her older brother, Theo, train. Two months prior to her ballet acceptance, she earned her black belt, one of the youngest ever at her club. Out of more than 1,000 applicants worldwide, only 24 were chosen for the Royal Ballet Schoolâs prestigious Lower School program, and Ava was among them. Starting in September, sheâll live away from home at White Lodge in Richmond Park, training full-time under some of the worldâs most renowned dance instructors. Her mother, Michele, describes Ava as someone who âdoesnât walk â she dances,â turning every hallway and sidewalk into a stage. Despite no family history in dance, Avaâs passion has driven her to master two physically demanding arts. Her father, John, and brother Theo, also a black belt, fully support her journey. article_content: In the aftermath of Haitiâs devastating 7.0-magnitude earthquake, a Belgian medical team evacuated a field hospital in Port-au-Prince on Friday night, citing urgent security concerns. The departure left CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta as the sole physician caring for more than 25 critically injured patients through the night. Initially, CNN reported that the United Nations had ordered the evacuation. However, Geert Gijs, the Belgian teamâs chief coordinator, clarified that the decision was his own. He said he requested UN peacekeepers to secure the facility overnight but was told they could only assist with evacuation. The team departed after a Canadian medical contingent â protected by its own security â had already left earlier that day. Gupta, aided by CNN staff, security personnel, and one Haitian nurse who refused to abandon her post, managed patients with no electricity, no blood supply, and dwindling medical equipment. He stabilized three new arrivals in critical condition, administered pain relief, and monitored vitals until dawn. The UN later denied issuing any evacuation order. Spokesperson Martin Nesirky affirmed that if teams left, it was their own choice. Edmond Mulet, UN Assistant Secretary-General for Peacekeeping, added that local security forces had declared the makeshift hospital unsafe. The Belgian team returned Saturday morning and has requested their government to deploy military personnel to safeguard the hospital â expected to arrive by Sunday evening. Meanwhile, critics including retired Army Lt. Gen. Russel Honore called the withdrawal âunforgivable,â comparing it unfavorably to the response during Hurricane Katrina, where medical staff never abandoned patients. With Haitiâs infrastructure shattered and hospitals overwhelmed, ambulances had nowhere else to take the wounded. Many suffered amputations, head trauma, and severe blood loss. Volunteers reported that most medical supplies were taken when the team left. As Gupta tweeted at 3:45 a.m.: 'Pulling an all-nighter at Haiti field hosp. Lots of work, but all patients stable. Turned my crew into a crack med team tonight.'

article_content: In a disturbing case from Afghanistan in 2011, a British Royal Marine commander, Sergeant Alexander Blackman, fatally shot a severely injured Taliban prisoner at point-blank range, telling him, 'Shuffle off this mortal coil, itâs nothing you wouldnât do to us.' Witnesses, including fellow Marines, did not intervene. Instead, they silently agreed to conceal the killing, knowing it violated the Geneva Conventions. The crime remained hidden for over a year until footage captured by Corporal Christopher Watsonâs helmet cam surfaced. This video triggered a military investigation. In 2013, Blackman, Watson, and Marine Jack Hammond faced court-martial for murder. While Watson and Hammond were acquitted, Blackman was convicted and sentenced to ten years â later reduced to eight on appeal. Initially, it was expected that Watson and Hammond, along with two other Marines originally charged, might face administrative penalties. However, recent defense sources confirm none of them will receive any further punishment. The Ministry of Defence acknowledges the case has been legally resolved through a public trial but says it is now reviewing broader procedures.

article_content: In a deeply emotional journey, Jerzy Dyczynski and Angela Rudhart-Dyczynski traveled from Perth, Australia, to the crash site of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 in eastern Ukraine. Their 25-year-old daughter, Fatima, was among the 298 people killed when the Boeing 777 was shot down over the village of Hrabove on July 17, 2014. Despite the danger and instability in the area â still controlled by pro-Russian separatists â the couple crossed into the region to fulfill a promise they made to Fatima: to return to the place where she lost her life. Walking among the scattered wreckage of the plane, now surrounded by grazing cattle and untouched for over a week, they searched silently for any trace of their daughter. 'We promised her weâd come here,' Angela said, tears in her eyes. Jerzy added, 'She believed in peace. And she will always be for peace.' Meanwhile, international efforts continue to recover and identify the victims. Two cargo planes transported 38 additional coffins from Kharkiv â a city under Ukrainian government control â to Eindhoven Military Airport in the Netherlands. There, the remains were moved in a solemn convoy of hearses, escorted by motorcyclists, to a forensic facility where official identifications will begin. This marks the fourth wave of repatriations coordinated by the Dutch, who have taken the lead in handling the tragedyâs aftermath. The aircraftâs black boxes have also been safely transferred to experts in the UK for analysis. The international community remains divided. The United States and Ukraine assert the plane was hit by a surface-to-air missile fired from rebel territory, likely supplied or supported by Russia. In response, the European Union imposed fresh sanctions targeting senior Russian officials, including heads of the FSB and SVR, freezing assets and banning travel. Russia retaliated sharply, claiming the sanctions undermine global security cooperation and even 'encourage terrorists.' As Ukrainian forces push closer to Donetsk â a key rebel stronghold â tensions continue to rise, with reports of Russian artillery crossing the border. Amid the chaos, families mourn, nations argue, and the world watches.

Hammond is among roughly 100 UK owners affected by the advisory. Porsche, prioritizing safety, is offering to collect the vehicles and transport them to authorized centers for inspection. The company emphasized that safety is its top concern and that it takes its responsibilities seriously. article_content: Liberty Ross, a former British fashion model, has been awarded a multi-million-pound settlement in her divorce from film director Rupert Sanders after he was caught in an affair with actress Kristen Stewart in 2012. The emotional betrayal came to light when photos of Sanders embracing Stewart in a Hollywood parking lot were published. Ross, 35, was reportedly devastated â learning of the affair just 20 hours before the images went public. In court documents filed in Los Angeles Superior Court, Ross secured a highly favorable financial arrangement. She retains ownership of three of the coupleâs four homes â including their Â£1.2 million property in the Hollywood Hills and two residences in London â while Sanders keeps only the Malibu home, a 1970 Volkswagen van, and a 2002 Nissan Pathfinder. Ross will receive Â£23,000 per month in combined spousal and child support: Â£14,700 in spousal support until 2018 or her remarriage, and Â£8,235 monthly for their two children, ages nine and seven. She also receives 8% of Sandersâ annual gross income above Â£1 million and half of his pension. Reports suggesting she receives half of his credit card reward points lack legal precedent and are likely speculative. Notably, Ross is entitled to a portion of future earnings from Snow White And The Huntsman â a film in which she portrayed Stewartâs characterâs mother. The movie has grossed over Â£230 million worldwide. The couple shares joint custody of their children, with Sanders covering 75% of their educational and medical expenses. Ross was represented by renowned divorce attorney Laura Wasser, known for securing landmark settlements for celebrities like Angelina Jolie and Maria Shriver. Sanders, whose gross monthly income is listed at Â£88,000, issued a public apology following the scandal. His legal team did not contest the terms. Ross, who previously worked as a model in London and appeared in a 2002 Burberry campaign with Kate Moss, has since begun a relationship with music executive Jimmy Iovine, estimated to be worth over $1 billion.

article_content: At the Sandringham Flower Show, Prince Charles shared a memorable moment with Zephyr, a majestic bald eagle weighing 10 pounds 4 ounces and boasting a wingspan of 7.5 feet â heavier than newborn Prince George. While wearing a protective glove, Charles gently held the bird, though he couldnât suppress a startled leap when Zephyr flapped her wings. Her handler, Lisa Falco of the Imperial Bird of Prey Academy in Essex, reassured onlookers that Zephyr was simply adjusting her balance. 'Sheâs incredibly calm,' Falco said, explaining that Zephyrâs name means 'gentle breeze' for good reason. Camilla, watching from a distance, declined any attempt to hold the bird. 'That beak is razor-sharp,' she remarked with a smile, opting out of the encounter. Meanwhile, the couple greeted hundreds of visitors braving steady rain, accepting thoughtful handmade gifts meant for the new royal baby. Ann Whiting presented a six-month labor of love: a crocheted shawl. Sheila Clarke traveled from Glasgow with a teddy bear embroidered with the name 'George.' A toddler, Evelyn Holt, offered blue crocus bulbs, telling Charles her hope that the flowers would grow as beautifully as her new cousin. The prince, visibly moved, said George was 'doing very well' and joked with well-wishers about whether they'd guessed the baby's name ahead of time. Among the crowd were celebrities including Dame Maggie Smith and Dame Judi Dench, who joined others enjoying the showâs floral displays and charity spirit. The event, held annually at Sandringham Park, raised funds for local causes â over half a million pounds since 1977. Charles also paused to admire a specially designed garden symbolizing the transformative work of the Princeâs Trust, where neglected land becomes thriving space â much like the young lives it supports. Scooby, a lively Jack Russell owned by Yvonne Harradine, became an unexpected star when Camilla happily posed for a second photo after a previous shot accidentally cropped her out. As umbrellas rose and smiles remained, the royal couple left by horse-drawn cart, leaving behind a day marked not by grandeur alone, but by quiet, heartfelt connections.

article_content: An Ohio grand jury has indicted 52-year-old Richard Beasley for the murders of three men who responded to a Craigslist job posting for work on a cattle farm. Authorities say Beasley was the principal offender in each killing, which occurred between August and November 2011. Beasley now faces 27 charges, including multiple counts of aggravated murder, kidnapping, aggravated robbery, grand theft, and identity fraud. Prosecutors argue he qualifies for the death penalty under Ohio law, due to the intentional killing of multiple victims, along with associated crimes such as kidnapping and armed robbery. One survivor, 48-year-old Scott Davis of South Carolina, escaped after being shot in the arm while fleeing. He told investigators he answered an ad for farm labor, met Beasley and another man, and was led to a remote wooded area in Stock Township, Ohio, where he was ambushed. Davis hid for seven hours before seeking help. The bodies of Ralph Geiger (56), David Pauley (51), and Timothy Kern (47) were later discovered in shallow graves. Authorities believe they were lured by the same Craigslist ad. Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine called the case a series of serial killings and urged the public to come forward with any informationâasking, 'Are there more bodies? We donât know.' Also charged is 16-year-old Brogan Rafferty, accused of helping dig graves and assist Beasley. His parents claim he was manipulated by Beasley, who allegedly posed as a chaplain offering aid to the homeless. Prosecutors are seeking to try Rafferty as an adult. A gag order has been placed on details surrounding Raffertyâs involvement. Beasley, who has been jailed since November 2011 on unrelated charges including drug trafficking and promoting prostitution, is scheduled for arraignment next Wednesday. DeWine warned that the case highlights the hidden dangers of online classifieds, saying, 'Technology was weaponized to prey on vulnerable people.'

article_content: Dan Maurer, a 39-year-old man from Battle Creek, Michigan, has successfully undergone surgery to remove a 120-pound growth caused by scrotal lymphedema â a rare condition in which blocked lymphatic vessels lead to severe fluid buildup. The 14-hour procedure, performed at the University of California, Irvine on August 28, also removed excess abdominal fat, resulting in a total weight loss of 150 pounds. For over a decade, Maurerâs condition progressed slowly, initially misdiagnosed as obesity. Despite losing 50 pounds through daily swimming, the swelling continued to grow until his scrotum became so large it nearly reached his ankles. His quality of life deteriorated, and he and his wife, Mindy, had not been intimate for seven years. After watching a TLC documentary about Wesley Warren Jr., another man with the same rare condition, Maurer recognized his symptoms and sought out Dr. Joel Gelman, the urologist who had treated Warren. Although the surgery was not covered by insurance, a GoFundMe campaign raised over $27,000 to make the operation possible. Maurer described the surgery as a matter of life and death, expressing fear of losing his penis alongside hope for renewed intimacy and mobility. His mother, Connie, shared that while he expected to leap out of bed post-op, he is now taking slow, deliberate steps in recovery, undergoing physiotherapy and expected to return home within a month. His father remarked that this marks the beginning of a 'whole new life' for Dan. Mindy has remained by his side throughout recovery. Dr. Gelman, who performed the surgery free of charge in Warrenâs case, did the same for Maurer â a gesture that has deeply moved the family.

article_content: A former professor of Barack Obama has turned against his one-time student and publicly urged voters not to re-elect him. Roberto Unger posted a video on YouTube detailing why he believes President Obama does not deserve a second term. Mr. Unger, a prominent Brazilian politician and former adviser to Obama during the 2008 campaign, stated: 'President Obama must be defeated in the coming election. He has failed to advance the progressive cause in the United States.' The 65-year-old academic, who maintained frequent contact with Obama via BlackBerry during the 2008 campaign, now disagrees with the Presidentâs policy direction. In his video titled 'Beyond Obama,' Unger delivers a scathing critique of Obamaâs economic policies, claiming they consist solely of 'financial confidence and food stamps.' He added: 'He has spent trillions of dollars to rescue moneyed interests and left workers and homeowners to their own devices.' While acknowledging that a Romney victory would bring costs in judicial and administrative appointments, Unger reserves his harshest criticism for Obama, asserting: 'He has evoked a politics of handholding, but no one changes the world without a struggle.' Unger summarized the past four years as: 'Give the bond markets what they want, bail out the reckless so long as they are also rich, use fiscal and monetary stimulus to make up for the absence of any consequential broadening of economic and educational opportunity, sweeten the pill of disempowerment with a touch of tax fairnessâeven though the effect of any such reform is sure to be modest.' He argued that Obama subordinated broader economic and educational equity to healthcare reform, mistakenly believing this would spare him political conflict. Unger also contends that the Democratic agenda is little different from the Republican oneâaiming merely 'to put a human face on the programme of its adversaries.' He concluded: 'Only a political reversal can allow the voice of democratic prophecy to speak once again in American life.' A renowned scholar and author of dozens of books on economics, philosophy, and politics, Unger has taught at Harvard Law School since 1976. Obama studied under him in 1988, focusing on jurisprudence and reinventing democracy. Unger, a founding member of Brazilâs Democratic Movement Party and former Minister of Strategic Affairs, has twice run for president of Brazil and advised governments across Latin America. The video, posted three weeks ago, has been viewed over 22,000 times. Separately, last week, the Obama administration announced a policy change affecting up to 800,000 undocumented young immigrants, halting deportations for qualifying individuals. Obama also faced criticism for combining official duties with fundraising events, raising $4.5 million at venues including Sarah Jessica Parkerâs home and the Plaza Hotel. However, the campaign offset costs by scheduling a brief stop at the World Trade Center site.

article_content: An Edinburgh councillor is pushing for a bold new plan to combat dog waste in the city: a DNA database that links every pet to its owner. Under the proposal, dog owners would be required to register their animals with the city and provide a simple cheek swab to store their dogâs genetic profile. If stray feces are found on streets, council wardens could collect a sample, run a quick DNA test, and match it to the registered owner â who would then face an Â£80 fine. Councillor Christopher Cowdy, a Conservative member, says current enforcement has failed: despite having the power to issue penalties since 2021, only four fines have been handed out. With roughly 13,000 dogs in the city and 24% of households owning one, he argues the problem is real â even if public complaints are few. The councilâs own data suggests most people donât report fouling because they know nothing gets done, not because itâs not happening. Cowdy admits the system could take years to roll out and acknowledges that some irresponsible owners may refuse to register. Still, he believes Edinburgh could become a pioneer in solving a nationwide nuisance. The city council confirms the idea is technically possible and is now studying costs, funding options, and whether fines could cover operational expenses. Meanwhile, Transport and Environment Convener Councillor Scott Arthur stressed that tackling dog waste remains a priority â and while the DNA database is under consideration, other measures are also being explored, including better cleaning services and public awareness campaigns.

article_content: On December 28, 2012, Carrie Mattingly, 43, lost control of her SUV on an icy road and plunged into a frozen lake with her five-year-old daughter, Ava, inside. As the vehicle slowly sank, both managed to escape through the driverâs side window. Just then, Jeff Oliver and several coworkers happened to drive by. Without hesitation, Oliver removed his boots and dove into the frigid water. Though the cold forced him to pause halfway, he returned and reached the sinking car. Other bystanders also jumped in, forming a human chain to pass Ava to safety. Oliver successfully grabbed her hand, pulled her through the water, and brought her to shore where others rushed to assist. After Ava was safe, Mattingly swam toward the bank. Oliver, who had also been pulled from the water, ended up in the same ambulance as mother and daughter. He later revealed he knew Mattinglyâs husbandâbut had never met her before that day. Mattingly suffered minor bruising; Ava was unharmed. Initially reported as 60â80 feet deep, the lakeâs depth was later confirmed to be only 10â15 feet. Reflecting on the ordeal, Mattingly told Fox59, 'Thatâs all I can think aboutâhow did we survive? Thank God we did. I need to make it to church every Sunday.' She said the experience transformed her perspective on life and family. Oliver simply said, 'I donât know what it takesâI just know you canât sit there and watch someone die. You have to try to help as much as you can.'

article_content: By Jaya Narain. PUBLISHED: 06:15 EST, 10 October 2012. | UPDATED: 20:16 EST, 10 October 2012. A mother who refused to pay a fine for taking her son out of school during term time to attend her wedding in the Caribbean will appear before magistrates next week. Frances Harden, 31, was denied permission to take her 13-year-old son, Harrison, out of school for the April wedding but went ahead anyway. Upon returning from the 14-day trip, she was fined Â£50. She believes the schoolâs decision was unreasonable and has refused to pay the local councilâs anti-truancy penalty on principle. As a result, the fine has doubled to Â£100, and she has now been summoned to court. Frances Harden stood at the altar in St Lucia alongside her husband, Nick Harden, with Harrison walking her down the aisle. Her younger son, Alex, then six, was permitted by his primary school to attend the ceremony. Mrs Harden, a care assistant from Stockport, began planning her Â£8,000 beach wedding at a four-star resort in St Lucia in 2011. She had assumed the event would coincide with Harrisonâs Easter break but later realized it would fall during term time. She repeatedly emailed the headmistress of Marple Hall School, Dr Rose Hegan, seeking permission but was denied one month before the wedding. Alexâs school granted him leave, creating a perceived inconsistency in policy application. When appearing before Stockport magistrates, Mrs Harden will face a charge of failing to ensure her sonâs regular school attendance. She plans to represent herself and expects a Â£1,000 fine. 'The system is inconsistent,' she said. 'Iâm refusing to pay the fine on principle. I want to make a point. I didnât have a problem with Alexâs school â they embraced it.' A spokesperson for Marple Hall School stated it must follow local authority and government guidance, which permits term-time holidays only in exceptional circumstances. Stockport Council added: 'Schools are closed for 13 weeks a year, providing ample opportunity for holidays and family events outside term time. Term-time absences without approval may result in fixed-penalty fines.'

article_content: The body of Mary Kennedy, the estranged wife of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has been reinterred on a sunny hillside in a different section of St. Francis Xavier Cemetery in Cape Cod, Massachusetts â two months after she was originally buried there, her family said. Kennedy, who had been battling depression, was found dead on May 16 in Bedford, New York, a small town north of New York City where she lived. The medical examinerâs office determined her death resulted from asphyxiation due to hanging. She was 52. The decision to relocate her grave was made because the original plot was tightly surrounded by other graves with no room for expansion, according to Kennedy family spokesman Ken Sunshine. Toxicology results showed no alcohol in her system. 'The grave is now on a sunny hillside, shaded by an oak tree, in an area with space for her children and other family members,' Sunshine said. Kerry Kennedy, Maryâs sister-in-law and close friend, along with two of Maryâs children, selected the new gravesite last week. Family members have since purchased approximately 50 plots surrounding the grave, including reservations for all six of Mary and Robert Kennedy Jr.âs children.

article_content: MediaTek and Qualcomm are close rivals competing for dominance in the Android smartphone market. Itâs no surprise, then, that the newly announced MediaTek Dimensity 8300 SoC bears striking similarities to Qualcommâs Snapdragon 7 Gen 3, unveiled just a week earlier. Following its flagship Dimensity 9300 launch, MediaTek wrapped up its recent media summit by introducing the more affordable Dimensity 8300. Built on a 4nm process, the chip features Armâs Armv9 CPU architecture with four Cortex-A715 and four Cortex-A510 cores â identical to those used in the Snapdragon 7 Gen 3. While Qualcomm officially clocks one A715 core at 2.63GHz and the other three at 2.4GHz, leaked data from Digital Chat Station (via Gizmochina) suggests the Dimensity 8300 may reach up to 3.35GHz for the primary core and 3.2GHz for the others â significantly outpacing Qualcommâs figures. A Geekbench listing from Notebookcheck, attributed to an unreleased Redmi K70, supports these clock speeds, though official confirmation remains pending. The Dimensity 8300 also incorporates Armâs Mali-G615 GPU, which MediaTek claims is 60% more powerful and 55% more energy-efficient than the GPU in its predecessor, the Dimensity 8200. The most significant leap, however, lies in AI performance: MediaTek asserts a 3.3x overall AI boost and an eightfold improvement in transformer-based generative AI capabilities, positioning the chip to better handle large language models like Metaâs Llama 2. Despite recent controversies surrounding AI leaders such as OpenAI and Google Gemini, demand for on-device AI is projected to grow steadily. Additional specifications include LP5x RAM at 8533 Mbps, UFS 4.0 storage, and Wi-Fi 6E with 160MHz bandwidth. Although no confirmed devices have been announced, MediaTek expects the Dimensity 8300 to appear in smartphones before the end of 2023. Given its limited presence in North America, the chip is likely to debut in devices from Asian manufacturers such as OPPO, Vivo, and Redmi â the same brands that previously adopted the Dimensity 8200.

article_content: When Shelley Lamond lost her daughter Mabel to stillbirth in May 2013, she wasnât ready to say goodbye. At the Adelaide hospital where she gave birth, staff provided her with a 'cuddle cot' â a refrigerated bassinet that allows parents to keep their stillborn baby in the room, delaying the need to move the infant to the morgue. Those extra 48 hours with Mabel meant everything to Shelley and her husband Rick. Moved by the experience, they began fundraising to donate another cuddle cot for other grieving families. Almost a year later, while four months pregnant again, Shelley donated a cuddle cot to a local charity â only to become its first user when she lost her second daughter, Elsa, to stillbirth on May 16, 2024, at 18 weeks and three days. 'They had the cot there,' she said, 'but I never expected Iâd be the first one to use it.' Having endured four stillbirths in total â Matilda in 2009, Pearl in 2012, Mabel in 2013, and Elsa in 2024 â Shelley knows the agony of losing a baby without the comfort a cuddle cot provides. Without one, she recalls being forced to wait while nurses retrieved her baby from the morgue in a canvas bag. 'Seeing my child in a green canvas bag... that was awful,' she said. She believes many parents â even those whoâve experienced stillbirth â remain unaware of cuddle cots because the topic is too painful for society to discuss openly. 'Itâs not the natural order,' she noted. 'People havenât met the baby, so they pretend it didnât happen. But it did.' Jan Samuels, CEO of Stillbirth Foundation Australia, confirmed cuddle cots are rare in hospitals due to their $5,000 price tag and low prioritization in funding. 'Usually, itâs grieving parents who raise the money to donate one,' she said. Meanwhile, Joanne Stephenson from Sydney lost her daughter Amelia in August 2023. She had no access to a cuddle cot and spent only seven precious hours with Amelia â bathing her, dressing her, reading her a poem. Later, her coworkers raised $8,000. With that money, she donated a cuddle cot to Sutherland Hospital. Since then, other mothers have reached out to thank her â one spent 36 hours with her baby thanks to the device. Now 39 weeks pregnant with her second child, Joanne says the journey has been emotionally overwhelming. She kept her pregnancy private for months, afraid to let others celebrate before she felt ready herself. But after marking Ameliaâs first birthday, she says she feels stronger. 'Iâm ready,' she said. In Australia, six babies are stillborn every day â affecting 2,200 families annually, or one in every 135 births. In nearly half of these cases, the cause remains unknown. Both Shelley Lamond and Joanne Stephenson continue to advocate for wider access to cuddle cots â and are raising funds to donate more.

article_content: As the election draws closer, a small but vocal group of openly conservative celebrities in Hollywood has intensified their political rhetoric. While some, like Vince Vaughn, quietly endorsed Ron Paul early on â a move both refreshing and, sadly, politically irrelevant â most media coverage has focused on the increasingly outlandish statements of aging stars. Chuck Norris condemned President Obama for allowing gay scouts, while Ted Nugent claimed history might have been better if the Confederacy had won the Civil War. Jon Voight rallied to defend Brad Pittâs mother after she wrote a letter calling Obama 'a liberal who supports the killing of unborn babies and same-sex marriage.' The modern Republican celebrity archetype seems to be a retired action star: cowboy-hatted, cigar-smoking, and politically positioned even further right than the Tea Party. Thereâs nothing inherently wrong with these views â but their public expression often feels less like thoughtful conservatism inspired by Edmund Burke and more like a midlife crisis manifesting as political outrage. When the Iraq War began in 2003, Bruce Willis reportedly called the White House offering to enlist â only to be told he was 'too old.' This anecdote captures the disconnect between myth and reality in todayâs Hollywood conservatism. Yet this wasnât always the case. In 1944, Cecil B. DeMille hosted a lavish gala for Republican nominee Thomas Dewey, attended by Ginger Rogers, Gary Cooper, and Barbara Stanwyck. During the McCarthy era, Hollywood grew more conservative. Actor George Murphy became a Republican senator in 1964; Ronald Reagan followed as Californiaâs governor in 1966. Richard Nixon, elected in 1968, embodied a Golden Age conservatism: he disliked profanity in film and walked out of 'West Side Story,' believing it was anti-American. His 1972 reelection fundraiser for Hollywood elites was described as 'a cocktail party at the Hollywood Wax Museum.' The guest list â Frank Sinatra, Charlton Heston, Glen Campbell, Clint Eastwood, Jack Benny, Jimmy Durante, George Hamilton, and Sammy Davis Jr. â was a whoâs who of established talent. Most were former Democrats; the dress code was tuxedos, not denim. Nixon understood that as liberalism grew trendy among youth, conservatism was becoming a countercultural movement. Thatâs why he tapped Clint Eastwood â the iconic 'Man With No Name' â as a delegate, while John Wayne narrated the film introducing Nixon at the convention. Eastwoodâs rugged persona symbolized the silent majority: self-reliant, law-and-order, and suspicious of government handouts. This alignment wasnât accidental. As Hollywood drifted left culturally, studios produced films like 'Dirty Harry' and 'Death Wish' that tapped into suburban fears of crime â aligning entertainment with conservative anxieties. Actors arenât just performers; theyâre brands. Sean Penn embodies liberal moral outrage; Alec Baldwin plays the fiery political aspirant; Betty White became a LGBTQ+ icon. These personas extend far beyond the screen. Even Clint Eastwoodâs brand is fluid: his 2008 film 'Gran Torino' was hailed as a 'red-state movie,' yet his 2012 Super Bowl ad 'Halftime in America' was accused by some Republicans of subtly promoting Obamaâs message. Branding isnât fixed â it adapts to the market. Todayâs Hollywood conservatism mirrors the Tea Partyâs culture-war ethos. The GOP no longer represents the establishment figures of Dewey or Nixon. It now champions populism and working-class resentment â and its celebrity icons reflect that shift. Sometimes, those icons become so consumed by their image that they turn into caricatures. Is it not absurd that 'The Expendables 2' celebrates violent septuagenarians as heroes? Many of these conservative stars seem incapable of even a spirited game of bridge at a retirement home. The deeper tension lies in how these brash, anti-elitist figures fit alongside Mitt Romneyâs preppy, elite persona â aimed at independents. They donât fit. And thatâs precisely one of Romneyâs problems heading into November.

article_content: As the European Union expands into Eastern Europe and the Balkans, Serbian Prime Minister Ivica Dacic is confident his country will be the next member. 'We want Serbia to join the EU as quickly as possible,' he told CNN. Serbia aims to become the third former Yugoslav nation to enter the EU, following Slovenia and Croatia, which joined earlier this year. But Dacic warns thereâs little time to waste: Serbiaâs economy has suffered deeply since the 1990s breakup of Yugoslavia. 'Unemployment is our biggest challenge,' Dacic said, pointing to a 25% jobless rate â second only to Spain and Greece among EU nations. He added that meaningful economic reform is impossible without a boost in industrial productivity. Foreign investment, he stressed, wonât come unless Serbia is fully integrated into the modern global economy. 'This isnât about handouts â itâs about belonging,' he said. According to Eurostat, Serbiaâs economy shrank by 1.7% in 2012, partly due to its economic ties with struggling eurozone countries. With a minimum wage lower than Chinaâs and a growing exodus of skilled workers, the country increasingly relies on money sent home by expatriates. EU membership could unlock vital funding for infrastructure and underdeveloped regions. Yet Dacic clarified: 'We donât see this as a financial aid package or a ticket for our people to work elsewhere in Europe.' The path to membership is long: Croatia began formal talks in 2005 and joined in 2013. Experts estimate Serbiaâs journey will take 8â10 years. Montenegro, which has already launched negotiations, may join first â its reforms are progressing faster. Serbiaâs biggest hurdle remains Kosovo. After Kosovo declared independence in 2008, Serbia refused to recognize it. The EU is mediating talks between the two, urging normalization before accession. 'We wonât drag our problems into the EU,' Dacic said. 'We must solve them first.' The Kosovo conflict, which erupted violently in the late 1990s, still casts a shadow. Analyst William Bartlett argues that EU membership could ease regional tensions, lowering investor risk and boosting Serbiaâs economy. 'Integration doesnât just change borders â it changes mindsets,' he said.

article_content: A Ukrainian freelance journalist, Anton Skiba, remains in detention two days after being seized by pro-Russian separatists in Donetsk. He was taken outside the Donbass Palace Hotel on Tuesday evening, shortly after working with a CNN crew covering the MH17 crash site. Armed men led by Alexander Kalyussky, a senior official in the self-declared Donetsk Peopleâs Republic (DPR), accused Skiba of terrorism and of posting cash rewards for killing separatist fighters on Facebook. Kalyussky presented printed documents he claimed were evidence, including a screenshot of Skibaâs Facebook page. Skiba was forcibly escorted into a vehicle without resistance. During the detention, Kalyussky confiscated the cell phone of CNN cameraman Jeff Kehl, who had been filming. He later apologized and returned it, but only after demanding the video be deleted. CNN, which had been quietly negotiating Skibaâs release through multiple separatist channelsâincluding contacts in the office of former DPR Prime Minister Alexander Borodaiâchose not to publicize the incident until efforts failed. Now, the network is publicly demanding Skibaâs immediate release. Kalyussky later dropped the terrorism allegations, claiming instead that Skiba was being questioned over possessing multiple IDs with different surnames. On Wednesday, another DPR official told CNN that Skiba had confessed to being a 'Ukrainian agent.' It remains unclear if this statement was coerced. The U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, Geoffrey Pyatt, condemned the detention, blaming Moscow for using disinformation and fear to destabilize Ukraine. article_content: Despite some high-profile investors trimming their positions, Salesforce has seen a surge in overall investor interest during the third quarter, fueled by a 64% jump in its stock price since January. Regulatory filings reveal that hedge funds Sachem Head Capital Management and Farallon Capital Management both increased their stakesâby 33% and 30% respectivelyâadding to their holdings as of September 30. This comes after both had reduced their positions in the previous quarter, suggesting renewed confidence in the companyâs direction. Salesforce has successfully addressed long-standing concerns raised by activist investors earlier in 2023. Key movesâincluding slashing costs, ramping up share buybacks, dissolving its M&A committee, and bringing Mason Morfit of ValueAct Capital onto the boardâhave quieted critics and reassured shareholders. While Starboard Value, one of the earliest voices calling for change, further reduced its stake by 14% in Q3 (following a 20% cut in Q2), other investors appear to believe the worst is behind the company. Even so, not all investors are bullish. Light Street Capital slashed its holding by 44%, and Polen Capital trimmed its position by 3.2%. These reductions reflect a broader caution among some asset managers, even as Salesforce continues to climb. The companyâs stock closed at $221.18 on November 15, maintaining its upward momentum despite minor pullbacks during the quarter. Although 13-F filings reflect past positions, they remain a vital barometer for how institutional players view Salesforceâs evolutionâfrom a targeted firm under fire to a restructured tech leader gaining traction.

article_content: Kyiv, Ukraine (CNN) â A shell landed near School 57 in Donetsk on Wednesday morning as children began the school year in this war-weary eastern Ukrainian city, killing at least three adults and shattering hopes for a return to normalcy for dozens of students. Around the same time, another shell struck a public transit bus in the city, killing six people in or near the vehicle, according to city officials. The attacks occurred despite a ceasefire agreement reached last month between Ukraineâs government and pro-Russian separatist leaders. The shell hit approximately five meters from School 57 at around 10 a.m., breaking windows and doors on the first and second floors. This was the first day of school in rebel-controlled areas of the Donetsk region â a start delayed by a month due to persistent shelling and clashes between separatists and Ukrainian forces. Reports on the number of fatalities at the school varied: officials at the rebel-run city administration stated that a biology teacher and two parents were killed, and five others were injured.

article_content: In the months leading up to the Japanese debut of 'The Boy and the Heron,' Studio Ghibli made a deliberate effort to keep details about Hayao Miyazakiâs latest animated feature to a minimum. For those trying to avoid spoilers, it has become increasingly difficult due to the growing buzz from its film festival circuit appearances. However, despite expectations that the trailer for GKidsâ English dub would reveal much, it offers a surprisingly restrained and tantalizing glimpse into what has captivated audiences. The trailer doesnât clearly establish where or when young protagonist Mahito (voiced by Luca Padovan) is in the story, but it is evident that the strange, inexplicable events surrounding him are tied to a mysterious talking grey heron (voiced by Robert Pattinson), which seems to know intimate details about his mother. Confused by recurring dreams in which his mother calls out for help, Mahito is even more unsettled by the heronâs uncanny awareness of his inner thoughtsâand its insistence that he follow it to a magical realm. Without explicitly outlining the plot, the trailer captures the sense of wonder that envelops Mahito as the grey heron leads him away, in classic Miyazaki fashion. It also provides just enough of the English dubâs vocal performances to suggest that 'The Boy and the Heron' will resonate strongly with U.S. audiences upon its theatrical release on December 8.

article_content: According to Campus Pride, a leading national LGBTQ+ campus advocacy organization, Chick-fil-Aâs WinShape Foundation has not funded the most controversial anti-same-sex-marriage groups since 2011. Campus Pride obtained access to WinShapeâs 2011 IRS Form 990 tax filings, which reveal that nearly $6 million in grants went toward youth programs, education, marriage enrichment, and local community initiatives. Notably, previously funded groups like the Family Research Council, Eagle Forum, and Exodus International no longer appear on the list of beneficiaries. Shane Windmeyer, Campus Prideâs executive director, acknowledged that WinShape still supports faith-based organizations â such as the Fellowship of Christian Athletes â that oppose same-sex marriage on biblical grounds. However, he emphasized that these groups do not engage in the same overt political activism as earlier recipients. The controversy erupted in July 2012, when Chick-fil-A President Dan Cathy told The Baptist Press, 'We are very much supportive of the family â the biblical definition of the family unit.' His remarks triggered nationwide backlash, with LGBTQ+ advocates calling for boycotts and politicians like Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel and former GOP presidential candidate Rick Santorum weighing in. In response, supporters rallied on 'Chick-fil-A Appreciation Day' (August 1, 2012), setting record sales for the chain. Days later, the Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation (GLAAD) organized 'National Same-Sex Kiss Day' at Chick-fil-A locations. Windmeyer noted that while campus protests on both sides intensified, few engaged in constructive dialogue. 'There was a lot of divisiveness and hate on both sides,' he said. 'It was like the Chick-fil-A brand was a chicken sandwich with purpose.' Neither Chick-fil-A nor the WinShape Foundation responded to requests for comment. According to its website, Chick-fil-A operates over 1,615 locations across 39 states and Washington, D.C., generating more than $4.1 billion in revenue in 2011. article_content: Four years after Hurricane Katrina, Biloxi, Mississippi, is still grappling with deep-rooted poverty and hunger â issues that have resurfaced as emergency aid faded. Rita Baldwin, who once lived on the streets herself, now leads Loaves and Fishes, a community kitchen that feeds hundreds daily. She recalls how Katrina temporarily erased social divides â 'It put us all on the same level.' But now, old attitudes are creeping back. Some locals have begun viewing the homeless with disdain, echoing harmful stereotypes like 'they're the scum of the earth.' Despite the cityâs visible progress â new homes at Keesler Air Force Base, a rebounding school system, and upcoming public projects â the human cost lingers. Loaves and Fishes served nearly 65,000 meals in 2008 alone. When federal disaster funds ran out, the kitchen nearly shut down. Only after a local newspaper exposed its plight did the community rally, donating over $50,000 to keep it open through early 2010. Clients include not only longtime homeless individuals but also displaced workers, elderly residents, and even tourists who lost everything gambling in Biloxiâs struggling casinos. One man, Terry, spent three years homeless after losing his home. He now rents a small room and relies on the kitchen for meals. His story reflects a quiet resilience: 'Weâre all trying to get back on our feet,' he says. 'But people are helping each other â and that matters.' While Biloxiâs unemployment rate has dropped from a crushing 23.2% after Katrina to 7.9% in mid-2009, itâs still a fragile recovery. Casino revenues have fallen, construction jobs have dwindled, and many locals say they were sidelined by out-of-town contractors during the rebuild. Mayor A.J. Holloway acknowledges the long road ahead, comparing recovery from Katrina to the decades-long effort after Hurricane Camille in 1969. 'Weâll feel the effects for a long time,' he says. For Baldwin, the mission is clear: hunger isnât far away â itâs right here. 'Thereâs not just hunger in Africa,' she insists. As the city prepares for $450 million in new infrastructure, she hopes compassion wonât fade again. 'People just didnât know,' she says, reflecting on the outpouring of support. And maybe, thatâs where real healing begins â not in concrete and steel, but in remembering weâre all in this together.
