article_content: On Wednesday night, the U.S. Senate approved a short-term government funding bill passed by the House on Tuesday night, narrowly averting a government shutdown just days before Fridayâs deadline. The vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: 87 in favor, 11 against â with 10 Republicans and one Democrat opposing the measure. The bill now heads to President Joe Bidenâs desk, and the White House has confirmed he will sign it into law. House Speaker Mike Johnson proposed a 'laddered continuing resolution' â a two-step funding plan that keeps government operations running at 2023 spending levels. Under this arrangement, funding for the Departments of Veterans Affairs, Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, Energy, and military construction will last until January 19. All other federal agencies remain funded until February 2. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had signaled early Wednesday that the chamber intended to collaborate with Republicans to expedite passage. Normally, Senate bills move slowly, but Schumer and Minority Leader Mitch McConnell worked together to accelerate the process. 'If both sides cooperate,' Schumer said earlier in the day, 'thereâs no reason we canât finish this bill today.' With a government shutdown looming just before Thanksgiving â a time when public and political tolerance for disruption is near zero â momentum built quickly. Although the White House had initially dismissed the GOPâs proposal as 'unserious,' urging House Republicans to prioritize the presidentâs supplemental aid request for Ukraine, Israel, border security, and humanitarian efforts, the stopgap bill does not include any of those additional funds.

article_content: Becoming a father didnât just change Khaled Hosseiniâs life â it reshaped his storytelling. His 12-year-old son recently posted a heartfelt review of his latest novel, 'And the Mountains Echoed,' on Goodreads, and the unexpected buzz helped grow his audience in ways Hosseini never anticipated. With a chuckle, he admits his son is at that tender age when kids begin to see their parents as real people â imperfect, complicated, human. Yet in this review, there was no hint of disillusionment, just pure admiration. It reminded Hosseini of his own journey from childhood reverence to adult understanding. That shift â the moment innocence cracks open to reveal complexity â is the heartbeat of his fiction. His novels, including the global hits 'The Kite Runner' and 'A Thousand Splendid Suns,' are rooted in Afghanistan, a land he left as an 11-year-old but has returned to repeatedly as a UNHCR ambassador. The story of two siblings torn apart by hardship, whose bond echoes across generations, was sparked by a quiet moment in 2009: a six-year-old girl in a remote village handing her younger sister an apple Hosseini had given her. 'It broke my heart,' he says. That gesture became the soul of his new book. Parenting, he believes, unlocked something in him â a deeper empathy for the impossible choices his characters must make. 'I write differently now,' he admits. 'I feel what they feel.' He dreams of taking Haris and Farah to Kabul one day, to walk the streets he once knew, to show them the school he attended, the neighborhoods he loved. Safety concerns have delayed the trip, but not the desire. Beyond writing, Hosseini channels his energy into his foundation, which supports refugee families and protects children in the rug-making trade. 'My characters arenât fiction to me,' he says. 'Theyâre the people Iâve met.' And though he doesnât go to Afghanistan looking for stories, the people, the pain, the tenderness â they seep into him. 'When I write,' he adds, 'theyâre there.' On World Refugee Day, he urged the world to stop seeing displaced families as numbers. 'Theyâre mothers, sons, daughters â just like us.'

article_content: A 52-year-old flamingo at Slimbridge Wetland Centre in Gloucestershire has baffled experts by adopting an unusual behavior to stay cool during Britainâs record-breaking summer heat. Instead of the typical method of standing on one leg and briefly dipping in water, this bird has taken to swimming with its legs stretched out behind it, resembling a floating pink swan. Keepers at the centre say they have never observed such behavior before. Paul Rose, a flamingo expert at WWT Slimbridge, noted: 'Lots of flamingos take quick paddles, but Iâve never seen anything like this. I first noticed it when the weather warmed up a few weeks ago â I believe itâs his way of cooling off during the hottest part of the day. He floats for long periods and seems completely relaxed. Itâs probably the equivalent of a human lounging on a float in a swimming pool.' An accompanying photo contrasts this behavior with the normal stance of an Andean flamingo in shallow water. Flamingos, known collectively as a 'flamboyance,' are found worldwide. There are six recognized species, and their distinctive pink or reddish plumage comes from carotenoid pigments in their diet â primarily from algae and crustaceans they filter from the water.

article_content: Meticulous preparation helped Pierluigi Collina become one of the greatest referees in football history. Before Chelseaâs 2005 Champions League clash with Barcelona at Stamford Bridge, he had studied every tacticâespecially how Chelsea exploited set pieces to aid John Terryâs aerial threat. 'Everything at corners was engineered to help Terry head the ball,' Collina recalled in an interview sparked by Sportsmailâs 'Hands Off In The Box' campaign, which seeks to curb illegal challenges in the penalty area. 'My focus? Terry. Always Terry.' In the 76th minute of the second legâwith the aggregate score tied 4-4 and Barcelona advancing on away goalsâDamien Duff delivered the corner. Collinaâs piercing gaze locked onto Terry as he rose. The ball met his head cleanlyâand went in. But Collina later admitted he missed a crucial detail: Ricardo Carvalho had shoved Barcelona goalkeeper Victor Valdes out of the way. 'If Iâd seen that, the goal wouldnât have stood,' he said. 'I couldnât be everywhere.' This moment became a turning point in Collinaâs advocacy for additional goal-line officials. As UEFAâs chief refereeing officer, he championed their introduction in the Europa League in 2009 and the Champions League in 2010. Since then, incidents of blocking and wrestling have sharply declined. 'Human error still happens,' he acknowledges, 'but weâve reduced the frequency and severity.' The added officials donât just improve detectionâthey deter misconduct. 'Itâs like driving past a police car,' Collina explained. 'Even if youâre not speeding, you slow down.' He cites cases where extra referees caught handballs missed by both the main ref and goal-line technology, such as in the May 2023 Scottish Cup final between St Johnstone and Hibernian. 'Tech sees the ball cross the line. A human sees the hand.' Collina also highlights Howard Webbâs use of additional officials in high-stakes matchesâEuro 2012 and Real Madrid vs. Bayern Munich (2023)âwhere critical decisions were corrected thanks to sideline communication. He argues that in incidents like the Oxlade-Chamberlain/Kieran Gibbs mistaken identity case in April 2023, an extra official could have prevented the confusion. Today, the system is standard across UEFA competitions and used in over 30 domestic leaguesâincluding Italy, Belgium, and Turkeyâfor key matches. Even skeptics like Jamie Carragher and Graeme Souness, after reviewing video evidence on a Sky TV show, became vocal supporters. 'The benefit,' Collina says, 'is clear: more control, fewer mistakes, fairer outcomes.'

article_content: Andre Bright, 30, is accused of murdering his girlfriend, Victoria Adams, 22, with a kitchen knife in their home in Oldham, Greater Manchester â just two days after she told friends she feared he would kill her. The crime occurred while their infant daughter slept nearby. According to court testimony, Bright had a history of violent and controlling behavior: he threw objects at her, spat in her face, and boasted about having sex with other women. On the night of December 5, 2013, after attending her first night out since giving birth, Adams fled in her dressing gown and bare feet to a friendâs house, terrified. Bright denied murder at his trial at Manchester Crown Court, claiming the killing was an accident caused by a psychotic episode. However, prosecutors argue the stabbing â one 8cm wound to the chest and a deeper 12cm wound penetrating her kidney â was deliberate and intentional. After the attack, Bright called emergency services, saying, 'Someone is dying in front of me...' But when pressed for details, he reportedly snapped, 'Shut up,' and hung up. When police arrived, Adams lay dying near the front door. Bright stood nearby with his hands in his pockets, staring blankly. Officers, fearing he still had a weapon, Tasered him. To their shock, Bright reportedly said, 'I enjoyed that. You need more volts in your Taser.' One officer described him smiling as he was placed in a police van. Bright, who had been involved in an on-and-off relationship with Adams since she was 16 and he was 23, also faces a separate charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm for attacking a bouncer in Oldham earlier that same night â an incident captured on CCTV, showing him stabbing the man repeatedly with a comb. Adamsâ baby daughter was found unharmed upstairs. Dozens of floral tributes have been laid at the scene. The trial, expected to last two weeks, continues.

article_content: CIA officials have asserted that former U.S. President George W. Bush fully authorized and was closely informed about the agencyâs 'enhanced interrogation techniques' used on suspected Al-Qaeda and Taliban operatives â directly contradicting findings in a recent Senate Intelligence Committee report. In response to the reportâs release, former Vice President Dick Cheney dismissed it as a 'terrible piece of work' and 'deeply flawed,' insisting that Bush not only knew about the program but personally approved its implementation. 'He was an integral part of the program,' Cheney told Fox News, urging viewers to 'read his book,' where Bush details his involvement. According to an anonymous CIA spokesperson, the program was not a rogue operation but a coordinated White House initiative. Key figures briefed included Vice President Cheney, White House Counsel Alberto Gonzales, National Security Advisor Condoleezza Rice, Deputy National Security Advisor Stephen Hadley, Attorney General John Ashcroft, and multiple Justice Department lawyers. Cheney acknowledged that Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was waterboarded 183 times but insisted this did not meet the legal definition of torture. He argued that such methods were essential to extract life-saving intelligence after 9/11, stating, 'We did exactly what needed to be done to prevent another attack.' While Cheney admitted that rectal feeding occurred, he claimed it was not among the 12 officially approved techniques. Still, he questioned, 'What are you prepared to do to get information about future attacks on the United States?' He defended the CIA operatives involved, saying they 'deserve credit, not condemnation,' and expressed no remorse for the programâs harshness, adding, 'I have no sympathy for them.' Cheney also noted that the CIA employed techniques previously used in training U.S. personnel â such as waterboarding in SERE programs â but emphasized that the application on detainees was far more intense and unregulated. article_content: Cyprus isnât just another Mediterranean getaway â itâs a living museum where myths walk beside ruins and cheese squeaks on your plate. Legend says Aphrodite, goddess of love, emerged from the sea near whatâs now called Aphroditeâs Beach. Locals swear the crashing waves form foam shapes that mirror her silhouette â though the siteâs real Greek name, Petra tou Romiou, honors a legendary warrior who hurled boulders into the ocean. Either way, itâs magical. Paphos doesnât just have ancient ruins â the entire town is a UNESCO-listed treasure. From 4th-century BC tombs carved into solid rock to stunning Roman mosaics discovered by chance in 1962, every corner tells a story. The mosaics? Think vibrant scenes of gods, seasons, and wine â like winter depicted as a grizzled elder sipping from a goblet. Commandaria, Cyprusâs sweet dessert wine, might be the oldest named wine on Earth. While crusaders gave it its name in the 1200s, locals say itâs been brewed for five millennia. King Richard I of England reportedly declared it 'the wine of kings and the king of wines' at his wedding â and honestly? He wasnât wrong. Carnival in Limassol is pure, unfiltered joy. Masked revelers, flamboyant parades, and a flamboyant Carnival King rolling through town on a gilded carriage â itâs Dionysus meets Mardi Gras, with a Cypriot twist. Donât expect to spot Cyprusâs national animal â the elusive mouflon. Once hunted nearly to extinction, these shy mountain sheep have rebounded thanks to conservation. You might catch a glimpse near Stavros tis Psorkas, but donât hold your breath â theyâre experts at hiding. Haloumi? That squeaky, salty, grillable wonder? Only Cyprus can make the real thing. Made from sheep or goat milk, brined with mint, and often homemade in village kitchens, itâs so protected that EU and U.S. laws say no other cheese can legally call itself haloumi. Dive lovers, listen up: the Zenobia shipwreck off Larnaca is a bucket-list site. This 1980s cargo ship, abandoned by its owners, now teems with fish and still holds decaying carpets and vending machines. Itâs eerie, beautiful, and utterly unique. And then thereâs the handkerchief tree. At the entrance to Paphosâs ancient catacombs, trees are draped in ribbons, scarves, and even socks â tied by people hoping for fertility, reconciliation, or a lost loverâs return. Itâs not folklore â itâs living ritual.

article_content: Secret Service Deputy Director Alvin 'A.T.' Smith has been removed from his position after 29 years with the agency, as part of a sweeping leadership overhaul following a series of high-profile White House security breaches. Smith, who managed the agencyâs day-to-day operations, will formally resign tomorrow but is expected to accept another unspecified federal position within the Department of Homeland Security, according to government officials. His removal follows the departure of six out of eight assistant directors last month and the resignation of former Director Julia Pierson in October. Acting Director Joseph Clancy described Smithâs contributions as 'invaluable,' while Department spokeswoman Marsha Catron confirmed Smith will join Immigration and Customs Enforcementâs Homeland Security Investigations unit, though his exact role and title remain undisclosed. Some members of Congress, including Utah Republican Rep. Jason Chaffetz, had previously criticized Smith, calling him 'a part of the problem, not part of the solution,' and questioned why he remained in office after the removal of other senior leaders. Chaffetz and Maryland Democrat Rep. Elijah Cummings both praised the agencyâs recent leadership changes. The Secret Service has faced mounting scrutiny after a string of embarrassing security lapsesâincluding a drone crash on the White House lawn, an armed intruder penetrating deep into the residence, multiple fence jumpers, and unauthorized guests at a state dinner. A December 2014 Department of Homeland Security review concluded the agency was 'starved for leadership' and suffering from low morale. Clancy stated the restructuring was 'necessary to gain a fresh perspective on how we conduct business.' article_content: Jailed: Kurt Delves, 23, was sentenced to three years and nine months for the unlawful killing of his daughter, two-month-old Harli Reid. A young father who shook his baby daughter to death after she wouldnât stop crying has been jailed for three years and nine months. Kurt Delves, 23, was sentenced today at Birmingham Crown Court for the unlawful killing of two-month-old Harli Reid on December 17, 2010. The court heard that Delves, from Birmingham, West Midlands, had been Christmas shopping with Harliâs mother, Donnika Reid, 30, when he returned home alone with the child. While bathing Harli before bed, Delves became frustrated when she continued to cry. He shook the infant, causing catastrophic brain injuries. Harli was rushed to Birmingham Childrenâs Hospital but died the following day. Delves initially fabricated a cover story, claiming Harli had become unwell in the bath and flinched after he splashed water on her face. He told police he had shaken her only lightly to try to rouse her. However, expert analysis proved the injuries were consistent with violent shaking â sufficient to cause fatal brain trauma. On the second day of his trial, Delves changed his plea to guilty on a charge of manslaughter. Sentencing him, Mrs Justice Thirwall said: 'Babies are vulnerable and defenceless â we all know that. They can often be noisy and demanding, but they are always vulnerable and defenceless. It is the duty of every parent to protect their tiny child. Harli was a much-loved and well-cared-for baby. Her mother did most of the care, but you were actively involved â changing nappies, giving bottles.' 'I accept you wanted to be a good father. But on December 17, 2010, you failed to protect Harli. Instead, you lost your temper and shook her repeatedly. For a brief moment, you shook her violently â you knew this would cause harm. She suffered catastrophic brain damage and died. A mother lost her child. Grandparents, including your own mother, lost a granddaughter. Her younger brother, born in January 2012, will never know her.' 'By pleading guilty, you acknowledge you lost your temper and shook her in the manner Iâve described. I accept it was brief, but the injuries were severe â including trauma to her neck â which, for a nine-week-old, is inherently violent.' Mrs Justice Thirwall sentenced Delves to three years and nine months in prison. Defending, Tim Raggat said: 'This is a tragedy for everyone involved. Medical reports show Delves is a deeply vulnerable man who will be especially vulnerable in prison.' Detective Constable Lyndsey Yates, who led the investigation, said outside court: 'Delves was described as very hands-on â often taking charge of bathing, feeding, and changing nappies. But in a moment of uncontrollable frustration, he snapped and shook his daughter in an attempt to silence her crying. He inflicted fatal injuries and then tried to conceal them with a false story. We exposed those lies. In the end, Delves had no choice but to admit what he did.'

article_content: Former First Lady Hillary Clinton now commands higher fees for public speaking engagements than her husband, Bill Clinton, and has a detailed list of logistical demands, according to newly released emails. The 67-year-old reportedly charged a $300,000 'special university rate' for a guest lecture at the University of California, Los Angeles, on March 5, 2014 â compared to the $250,000 her husband, former President Bill Clinton, received for his 2012 appearance at the same institution. Emails exchanged between her representatives and UCLA officials â later obtained by The Washington Post under a Freedom of Information Act request â reveal an extensive set of requirements. These included a backstage menu featuring diet ginger ale, cruditÃ©s, hummus, and sliced fruit; a case of still water at room temperature placed on stage; and a carafe of warm water, coffee cup and saucer, water glass, and lemon wedges. She also requested two long, rectangular pillows on her chair and insisted that any award presented to her be delivered in a box rather than draped around her neck. Additional demands extended to a secondary room where she would take photos with 100 VIPs or 50 couples â with only two group photos permitted, and those required to be pre-assembled so 'the Secretary of State isnât waiting for these folks to get their act together.' Five days before the event, her team rejected the originally planned podium, prompting UCLA to procure a replacement. Officials were also required to rent a new university seal to match the eventâs branding and purchase a computer, mouse, printer, and scanner for her use. When asked if she offered discounted rates for public universities, her team replied that $300,000 was the standard 'special university rate.' One UCLA administrator reportedly responded, 'Wow! She gets $50K more than hubby!' Clinton has defended her speaking fees, stating all proceeds go to the Clinton Foundation to support its global humanitarian efforts. She clarified that her earlier comment describing her family as 'dead broke' after leaving the White House in 2001 was 'inartful.' In interviews, she emphasized that her talks aim to promote economic ideas aimed at reducing income inequality, noting that audiences care more about their own struggles than her personal wealth.

article_content: An investigation reveals that Michael McIndoe, a former professional footballer, is accused of recruiting fellow players into an investment scheme falsely claimed to be managed by City financiers. Up to 100 footballers may have been defrauded of a total of Â£30 million, according to authorities. Former top-flight stars such as Robbie Keane and Jimmy Bullard are among those reportedly lured by promises of returns up to 20%, before the scheme collapsed under unsustainable debt. Detectives are now examining possible links between the fraud and illegal football match betting, as reported by the Sunday People. Police describe it as the largest financial scam ever targeting British football. A source close to the investigation stated that footballers collectively handed over as much as Â£30 million. The alleged fraud was reported to the National Fraud Bureau last year, and McIndoe â a 35-year-old ex-midfielder for Coventry, Wolves, and Scotland â is the primary focus. McIndoe declared bankruptcy in October, listing Â£3 million in debts. Experts suggest this figure is only the tip of the iceberg, with potential total losses reaching Â£15 million once all transactions are traced. One line of inquiry suggests the scheme functioned as a Ponzi scheme â where payouts to early investors were funded by money from later ones, a model destined to fail. The scandal emerged publicly after Jimmy Bullard appeared on the reality show 'Iâm A Celebrity...Get Me Out of Here!' in November. Reports linked his participation to financial distress following his loss of Â£625,000. He reportedly earned Â£100,000 from the show to help recover his losses. Ireland international Robbie Keane, now playing for LA Galaxy, lost 'a fortune,' according to sources. Another unnamed former teammate reported losing Â£100,000. One victim invested a Â£60,000 inheritance received in adolescence. The Metropolitan Police confirmed an allegation of fraud was filed with Westminster CID in February. No arrests have been made. Attempts to contact McIndoe through his registered business accounts have been unsuccessful. The Ponzi scheme, named after Italian immigrant Charles Ponzi, who ran a similar fraud in 1920s America, relies on new investor funds to pay earlier participants. article_content: Trials have begun in the UK for a promising new drug called irosustat, which may help extend the lives of thousands of women with advanced breast cancer. Designed to complement existing hormone therapies, irosustat aims to block a second pathway of estrogen production â a key fuel for approximately two-thirds of breast cancers. Led by Professor Carlo Palmieri of The Clatterbridge Cancer Centre, in collaboration with the Linda McCartney Centre at the Royal Liverpool Hospital and the University of Liverpool, the pioneering IRIS study is managed by Imperial College London, where the drug was also developed. After encouraging early results, 27 women are currently participating in the initial trial phase. Each receives irosustat alongside standard aromatase inhibitors like anastrozole. Professor Palmieri believes that if the trial proves effective, irosustat could be approved for clinical use within three years. He emphasized that it is a fully UK-developed treatment. One participant, diagnosed with secondary breast cancer nine years after a mastectomy, shared her motivation: 'I have seven young grandchildren â Iâll do anything to stay around for them.' She began treatment four weeks ago and remains hopeful. Aromatase inhibitors â including anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane â are currently prescribed to postmenopausal women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer to reduce estrogen levels and prevent tumor growth. Irosustat targets a different biological pathway, preventing conversion of a precursor hormone into estrogen.

article_content: A 90-year-old woman with dementia was left waiting on a trolley in a hospital corridor for five hours, according to family allegations. Pam Bailey, of Fareham, Hampshire, was taken to A&E in an ambulance suffering from a urinary tract infection, vomiting, and dehydration. Paramedics delivered her to Queen Alexandra Hospital in Portsmouth at approximately 6:20 p.m. She was placed on a trolley in a crowded corridor and remained there for five hours before being seen by a doctor. She then waited an additional four hours before being transferred to a ward. Mrs. Bailey, a former member of the Women's Royal Naval Service (Wrens), described the experience as deeply traumatic. She said, 'I'm pretty shook up â it feels like the wait has cut years off my life. I think the hospital owes us something, but I don't know what it is exactly. A simple 'sorry' would be a nice word for them to say to everybody. For two-and-a-half years during the Second World War I was in the Wrens and we never had treatment like that. I wouldn't want anyone else to go through what I had to that night.' Her daughter, Pauline Taylor, said staff repeatedly urged them to file a complaint, stating such delays were common. Photos taken during the wait were submitted as evidence. Mrs. Bailey, who lives independently despite a recent dementia diagnosis, was periodically monitored and received an IV drip nearly four hours after arrival. During her two-night stay, she was moved between two different wards. Her family reported she became confused and distressed, believing they had abandoned her. A hospital spokesperson confirmed an internal investigation is underway but cited patient confidentiality restrictions. According to NHS Trust data, Queen Alexandra Hospital failed to meet its target of treating 95% of A&E patients within four hours between September and December. In November, an average of three out of every 14 patients arriving at 6 p.m. waited longer than four hours. By contrast, nearby Southampton General Hospital averages six minutes from admission to triage.

article_content: Ed Miliband faced a fierce backlash from within the Labour Party last night after a poorly judged attempt to build rapport with Rupert Murdochâs Sun newspaper. The Labour leader, who had previously positioned himself as a critic of Mr. Murdoch during the phone-hacking scandal, sought to mend relations ahead of the next election by posing with a special World Cup edition of the tabloid. However, the image sparked outrage among Labour activistsâparticularly in Liverpool, where the newspaper remains boycotted over its controversial coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster. The backlash intensified as Labour councillors and MPs condemned the gesture. Liverpool councillor Martin Cummins resigned from the party, stating, 'Seeing Ed promoting The Sun has rocked me to my core.' Labour mayor Joe Anderson called the act 'an insult to every person in the city,' accusing politicians of being 'out of touch' with ordinary citizens. Liverpool MP Steve Rotheram welcomed Milibandâs apology but insisted he should never have allowed himself to be photographed with the paper. Miliband issued a public apology, saying he was 'very, very sorry' for causing offense. A Labour spokesperson clarified that his intention was to support Englandâs World Cup campaign, not endorse the newspaperâbut acknowledged the deep hurt caused by the association with The Sun. The controversy came amid broader turmoil for Miliband. His new slogan, 'Hardworking Britain Better Off,' was widely criticized at a meeting of the Labour National Executive Committee (NEC), with 98% of surveyed members reportedly hating it for appearing to stigmatize the unemployed. NEC member Ann Black called it 'divisive, meaningless' and 'sounding like a Tory slogan.' On immigration, senior Labour MP John Mann accused the leadership of being out of touch with working-class communities, claiming they fail to recognize the real impacts of mass migration. He warned that without a stronger stance, Labour would continue losing voters to UKIP in the upcoming general election. In a candid interview, Shadow Justice Secretary Sadiq Khan admitted that Labour is struggling to convince voters its policies are credible. 'The public just donât believe what we say,' he told the Huffington Post. 'The challenge isn't just having more policiesâitâs persuading people they can be delivered.'

article_content: In a move to ease trade tensions, Russia has reopened its borders to fresh vegetables from Belgium and the Netherlands, ending a ban that began after a deadly E. coli outbreak in Germany. According to Gennady Onishchenko, head of Russiaâs consumer protection agency, these two countries were chosen because their food safety labs are highly trusted and no local cases of the bacteria have been detected there. The Netherlands, which supplies roughly one-third of all fresh vegetables Russia imports from the EU, stands to benefit significantly from the decision. Exporters from both nations must now provide official certificates verifying the origin and safety of their produce. Meanwhile, five other EU countries â Poland, Lithuania, Spain, Denmark, and the Czech Republic â remain under review and could see their access restored if they meet Russiaâs new safety standards. The original ban followed an E. coli epidemic linked to contaminated sprouted seeds, which has claimed 47 lives across Europe, including one in Sweden. A new cluster of nine hospitalizations in Franceâs Bordeaux region appears to involve the same strain, though authorities say the source remains uncertain. French officials suggest the seeds may have come from a British firm, but no definitive connection has been confirmed yet. Last year, EU nations exported nearly â¬600 million worth of vegetables to Russia, highlighting the economic stakes involved.

article_content: Abigail Hernandez, a 15-year-old from Conway, New Hampshire, returned home safely after being missing for nine months â but authorities still have no answers about what happened. She vanished on October 9, 2013, while walking home from Kennett High School, sending texts between 2:30 p.m. and 3 p.m. before disappearing. Her reappearance on a Sunday in July 2014 was captured on security footage at a local train station. Police have released images of the clothing she wore upon return: a striped sweater, black pants, a camouflage backpack, and a drawstring bag. They are also reviewing surveillance videos and asking residents if they saw her or a woman matching that description between 10 p.m. and 10:30 p.m. that Sunday. Months before her return, Abigail mailed a letter to her mother, Zenya Hernandez, postmarked October 23 and received on November 6. Authorities delayed releasing details to verify its authenticity and avoid copycat incidents. The letter fueled speculation that she may have left willingly but was later coerced. FBI investigators, including Agent Kieran Ramsey, raised the possibility that Abigail was being manipulated â drawing a cautious parallel to the Cleveland kidnappings, though no direct connection was ever proven. The search for Abigail involved hundreds of volunteers, aerial patrols, riverboat searches, and the distribution of thousands of flyers. The Conway Police Department spent over $20,000 on overtime alone, not including unpaid hours from senior officers. Her motherâs heartfelt public letters â including a Christmas plea with a hand-drawn tree â became symbols of hope. Zenya repeatedly assured Abigail she was not in trouble and begged her to come home. The community, once united in prayer and search efforts, now seeks clarity. Residents like Andrew Berg and Jameson Proko, who kept mementos of the case, voiced frustration: 'I want answers. The truth often clarifies a lot of things.' State Attorney General Joseph Foster confirmed Abigailâs reunion with her family and quoted her mother: 'Today we are the happiest people on earth.' He added, 'Hopefully, her life gets back to normal â she goes back to school and everythingâs good.' While the criminal investigation remains open, police stress there is no evidence of foul play. Still, the unanswered questions linger â and so does the public demand for the full truth.

article_content: More than three decades after her body was discovered in a Bridgeport park, Estella Brantleyâs killer has finally been brought to justice. In 1980, the 30-year-old mother of two was found dead, strangled and partially clothed near the grassy edges of Seaside Park, a $50 bill resting beside her. For over 30 years, police suspected her murder was tied to a string of killings involving women in the areaâmany assumed to be sex workersâbut no suspect was ever identified. That changed last summer, when investigators turned to preserved DNA evidence from the crime scene. The sample matched Leonard Jackson, a 53-year-old man who had been incarcerated since 2006 for illegally discarding the body of a woman who died of a drug overdose. When confronted with the match, Jackson admitted to being present during Brantleyâs death. He told police he began arguing with her during a walk in the park after becoming angry over her seeing someone else. He claimed he struck her and later found her lying motionless on the ground, though he couldnât recall if he had strangled her himself. He expressed regret, saying, 'Iâm sorry.' Though neighbors reported hearing screams that night, no one called the police. Jackson, who had long been known to police for his association with sex workers, was never considered a suspect until the DNA breakthrough. At his arraignment, Brantleyâs daughter, Gwendolyn, spoke out: 'She wasnât just a name in a fileâshe was a mother who loved her children deeply.' Jackson remains jailed on $1 million bail, with court proceedings scheduled for August 28.

article_content: Nestled deep in Chinaâs Taihang Mountains, the Guoliang Tunnel is a breathtaking feat of human grit â entirely dug by hand by just 13 villagers over five grueling years. Before its completion in 1977, the remote village of Guoliang was accessible only by a terrifying 720-step stairway carved into a near-vertical cliff, with no railings, narrow paths, and deadly drops. To fund their dream, locals sold goats and medicinal herbs to buy basic tools: hammers, drill rods, and steel picks. What emerged was a 1,200-meter-long, 5-meter-high, and 4-meter-wide passage, wide enough for vehicles, with more than 30 uniquely shaped windows punched through the rock â some round, others square â offering stunning views and natural light. Opened on May 1, 1977, the tunnel transformed life for Guoliang, connecting it to the outside world and sparking a wave of tourism drawn to both its beauty and its story. Today, visitors marvel at how such an ambitious project was achieved without machinery, and often mistake it for Boliviaâs infamous North Yungas Road â a dangerous, single-lane highway known as the âRoad of Death,â which has no resemblance in design or location. The Guoliang Tunnel stands not as a tourist gimmick, but as a monument to quiet courage, community, and the power of persistence.

article_content: A high-profile trial at Londonâs Old Bailey has sparked debate over press freedom, as Nick Parker, The Sunâs chief foreign correspondent, faces charges related to his journalistic activities. Parker is accused of gaining unauthorized access to a mobile phone belonging to MP Siobhain McDonagh â which had been stolen from her car â after being told it contained evidence of criminal behavior, including bribery. He reportedly reviewed the messages but decided not to publish anything after concluding the content was clearly satirical. He then advised the source to hand the device to police. Parker is also charged with receiving confidential information from former officer Alan Tierney, who later admitted to misconduct and resigned. The information led to two widely reported stories: one detailing how police only issued a caution to John Terryâs mother following a Â£1,450 shoplifting incident, and another concerning Ronnie Woodâs assault on his partner. His defense team, led by Trevor Burke QC, argues these stories served the public interest and that prosecuting Parker for pursuing such reporting sets a dangerous precedent. Burke told the jury that targeting a journalist for doing his job â even if methods were ethically questionable â mirrors tactics seen in authoritarian states. 'Youâre being asked to punish someone for telling the truth,' he said. 'This isnât about breaking laws; itâs about silencing accountability.' Parker, 53, denies all charges and maintains he acted within journalistic norms. The trial continues as the jury weighs whether his actions cross the line between investigative reporting and criminal conduct.

article_content: A giant panda slated to be the star of the first-ever live broadcast of a panda birth has lost her role â after it was discovered she is not pregnant, Chinese state media reported. Not only was it a phantom pregnancy, but zookeepers suspect the panda, Ai Hin, may have been faking symptoms to improve her quality of life, the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding told Xinhua on Monday. Ai Hin, age six, showed signs of pregnancy in July, including changes in appetite, reduced movement, and elevated progesterone levels, according to Xinhua. But after nearly two months, she returned to normal behavior, zookeepers noted. Experts say pandas sometimes mimic early pregnancy behaviors after learning they receive preferential treatment â such as being moved to private, air-conditioned rooms with round-the-clock care and extra food like buns, fruits, and bamboo. 'After showing prenatal signs, the 'mothers-to-be' are moved into single rooms with air conditioning and around-the-clock care,' said Wu Kongju, an expert at the Chengdu base. 'They also receive more buns, fruits, and bamboo, so some clever pandas have used this to their advantage to improve their quality of life.' The live broadcast of Ai Hinâs cub â from its first cries to developing its iconic black-and-white fur â was planned for audiences across China and globally. Giant pandas are notoriously difficult to breed in captivity. Pseudo-pregnancies are common. Females are fertile for only about three days per year, and gestation lasts between 80 and 200 days, according to the Chengdu base. Even when pregnancy is confirmed, survival rates for newborns remain low. Only one-third to one-half of pandas born in Chinese captivity survive past infancy. Last month, however, there was cause for celebration: a panda at Chimelong Safari Park in Guangzhou gave birth to the worldâs only known living triplet cubs. Edinburgh Zoo in Scotland believes its panda, Tian Tian, may be pregnant, based on recent tests â but confirmation remains uncertain. 'It is very likely that we will not know 100% if Tian Tian is pregnant until she gives birth,' said Iain Valentine, director of giant pandas for the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland. According to the Smithsonian Institutionâs National Zoo, fewer than 1,600 giant pandas remain in the wild in central Chinaâs mountain forests. More than 300 live in zoos and breeding centers worldwide â most of them in China.

article_content: In October 2014, Spanish health officials made the controversial decision to euthanize Excalibur, the pet dog of Teresa Romero Ramos, a nurseâs assistant who contracted Ebola while caring for infected missionaries at Madridâs Carlos III Hospital. Though Romero and her husband were placed under observation â and neither showed symptoms beyond her confirmed diagnosis â authorities chose to put down the dog, citing concerns it might carry and spread the virus. The move sparked widespread outrage: a Change.org petition gathered nearly 400,000 signatures urging officials to quarantine Excalibur instead, arguing that if humans could be monitored, so could a pet. The dog was sedated and humanely euthanized, then cremated under strict biohazard protocols. Scientifically, the risk posed by dogs remains unclear. During the 2001â2002 Ebola outbreak in Gabon, researchers from the CDC detected antibodies in about 25% of local dogs, indicating exposure â yet none fell ill. Dr. Margaret H. Gilbert of Tulane noted this suggests dogsâ immune systems respond to the virus, but whether they shed infectious material â through urine, feces, or saliva â is still unknown. While Ebola is well-documented to jump from wildlife such as fruit bats and primates to humans, canine transmission has never been proven. Experts warn against assuming dogs are a threat without evidence, especially when less extreme options exist.

article_content: In 2011, acclaimed British writer Andrew OâHagan was commissioned by publisher Canongate to ghostwrite Julian Assangeâs autobiographyâa project that ultimately collapsed amid Assangeâs erratic behavior and growing resistance. OâHagan, a Booker Prize-nominated author, found his collaboration with the WikiLeaks founder to be a surreal mix of brilliance and chaos. Assange, he observed, was simultaneously courageous and cowardly, visionary and vain, generous and manipulative. Though initially enthusiasticâtelling OâHagan he wanted the book to read 'like Hemingway'âAssange became deeply unsettled as the deadline neared. He dismissed memoir-writing as the domain of 'prostitutes' and refused to engage meaningfully with the process. Canongate, frustrated by Assangeâs noncooperation, released an unauthorized version of OâHaganâs manuscript in September 2011 titled *Julian Assange: The Unauthorised Biography*. Assange did not approve itâbut secretly tweeted links to its Amazon page. The result? Fewer than 700 copies sold in its first week. During this period, Assange lived in relative luxury at Ellingham Hall, a Norfolk stately home, under conditions humorously dubbed 'mansion arrest' by his legal team. Surrounded by loyal supporters, he continued his activism: during Egyptâs 2011 uprising, he and his team hacked into government systems from their kitchen table to restore internet accessâthen casually ate chocolates as the revolution unfolded. OâHagan recounts how Assange reportedly believed Fidel Castro once called WikiLeaks 'the only website he liked,' and boasted that if Tony Blair could earn Â£120,000 for an hour of Skype, he deserved at least Â£120,001. Assangeâs relationships with media outlets were deeply fractured. He saw The Guardian and the New York Times as betrayersâfor publishing stories he deemed unfaithful to his visionâwhile oddly respecting the Daily Mail for its unrelenting hostility. Yet beneath the bravado, OâHagan glimpsed vulnerability: a man haunted by his own past, terrified of exposure, and emotionally stuck between rebellion and retreat. He describes Assange as a modern-day Peter Panâa 'lost boy of Queensland' with strikingly pale hair, unable to accept adulthood, and forever running from the consequences of his own truths.

article_content: At the heart of the Schengen Agreement lies the idea that people can travel freely across internal borders without checkpoints â a landmark achievement for European unity since its signing in 1985 aboard a small boat on the Moselle River near the village of Schengen. But the deal always had an escape hatch: if public safety or national security is at risk, countries can temporarily bring back border controls. In 2023, at least seven Schengen nations did exactly that. According to political scientist Eugenio Cusumano, these moves arenât just about security â theyâre often political theater. Governments use them to send a message: 'Weâre cracking down on migration,' especially as elections loom. And once one country does it, others often follow â a domino effect fueled by rising populist sentiment. Germany, for instance, restarted checks with Poland and the Czech Republic, claiming itâs targeting human traffickers. Slovenia ramped up monitoring along its border with Croatia, which just joined Schengen. Yet experts stress these arenât full border closures â most involve random spot checks affecting only a tiny fraction of travelers. Still, the symbolism matters. Meanwhile, Bulgaria and Romania have waited over 15 years to join Schengen, even though the European Commission and Parliament agree theyâve met all technical requirements. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called their inclusion 'without further delay.' But political resistance remains. The Netherlands and Austria oppose their entry, arguing they sit on the so-called Balkan Route, a major migration corridor. Yet critics argue this is less about security and more about reluctance to share responsibility. As Cusumano puts it: 'The Schengen system is perfectly fine â itâs one of Europeâs greatest successes.' The real challenge isnât the rules â itâs whether member states still believe in them.

article_content: Denmarkâs Nicklas Bendtner has been fined $125,800 and given a one-match suspension by UEFA for revealing boxer shorts bearing the logo of online betting company Paddy Power during a goal celebration against Portugal at Euro 2012. The Arsenal striker, who was on loan at Sunderland last season, lifted his shirt after scoring his second goal to display the branded undergarments. UEFA confirmed the disciplinary action in a statement, noting the violation stemmed from unauthorized commercial promotion. Bendtner told reporters he was unaware the act violated UEFA regulations, calling the underwear 'lucky' and saying heâd worn them in previous matches, including the tournament opener. The severity of the penalty has drawn widespread criticism online, particularly in light of lighter punishments for racist behavior earlier in the year. For instance, Portuguese club FC Porto was fined just â¬20,000 following fan racial abuse targeting Manchester Cityâs Mario Balotelli. Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand criticized UEFA on Twitter, questioning its priorities: 'If racism made money for UEFA like advertising does, do you think theyâd take it as seriously?' Paddy Power responded on social media, calling UEFAâs move 'hysterical and deeply cynical,' and announced plans to support Bendtner. The player has three days to appeal the decision.

article_content: For the first time since their escape, Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus, and Michelle Knight appeared together on stage at Ohio Governor John Kasichâs annual Courage Awards on Monday night. The three women, who survived a decade of horrific captivity under Ariel Castro in Cleveland, received a two-minute standing ovation from the audience. Governor Kasich praised them during his State of the State address, calling their story 'one of hurt beyond imaginationâbut also one of triumph.' He said, 'No one rescued them. They rescued themselvesâfirst by staying strong, sticking together, and then by breaking free.' Kidnapped between 2002 and 2004 at ages 16, 16, and 21, the women were held captive in a house on Seymour Avenue. They escaped on May 6, 2013, after Berry forced open a door and called 911. In a trembling but clear voice, she told dispatchers: 'Help me. Iâm Amanda Berry. Iâve been missing for 10 years. Iâm here. Iâm free.' Castro pleaded guilty to 937 counts including kidnapping, rape, and aggravated murder and was sentenced to life in prison plus 1,000 years without parole. He died by suicide in his cell on September 3, 2013, just weeks after sentencing. Since their rescue, the women have cautiously reentered public life. In July 2013, they released a joint video thanking supportersâthe first public appearance by Michelle Knight, whose kidnapping had previously been unknown. That same month, Berry appeared at a Nelly concert, DeJesus joined the Puerto Rican Parade, and Knight attended a Cleveland Browns game. At Castroâs August 2013 sentencing, Knight delivered a powerful statement: 'I spent eleven years in hell. Your hell is just beginning.' She described enduring daily torture, relying on her bond with DeJesus to survive. 'She never let me fall. I never let her fall.' In a November interview with Dr. Phil, Knight recounted being bound like a fish, and Dr. Phil called it the most harrowing moment of his 12-year career. Despite their trauma, the women have expressed gratitude for public support and requested privacy, declining media interviews. Governor Kasich hugged the women before his speech, and images of the embrace spread rapidly online. He called them 'three extraordinary women who rose above the worst the world could throw at themânot as victims, but as victors.' Their joint appearance marked not only a personal milestone but a powerful symbol of endurance, solidarity, and hope.

article_content: (CNN) -- Oprah Winfrey didn't pussyfoot around â she got Lance Armstrong to confess within the first minute. It was a strangely unemotional exchange, with Winfrey guiding Armstrong through what felt like a rehearsed script in a calm, businesslike manner. Armstrong apologized for years of deception, but his tone sounded mechanical, as if reading from a grocery list. Though he wore a lavender shirt that matched Winfreyâs violet dress, the disgraced cyclist was anything but vibrant. On her cable network Thursday night, Winfrey began with a series of direct yes-or-no questions that dismantled a decade of lies. Did Armstrong use banned substances? Yes. EPO? Yes. Blood transfusions? Yes. Did he dope during all seven Tour de France victories? Yes. If you switched channels, you didnât miss much. This was the most anticipated interview since Monica Lewinsky spoke with Barbara Walters â except there were no sex scandals, no audiotapes, just persistent falsehoods. Yet the event felt anticlimactic. Leaks had already revealed Armstrong was preparing to confess: first to the New York Times, then to USA Today, then to the Associated Press. All that remained was to see his wording and demeanor. He didnât seem contrite. 'You brazenly and deliberately denied everything youâve just admitted to me,' Winfrey said. Armstrong offered no rebuttal. 'You called other people liars.' True. Armstrong didnât engage â he endured. He admitted he couldnât have won without doping and claimed he never thought heâd get caught. But he never explained why he lied so relentlessly. 'The story was so perfect for so long,' Armstrong said. Indeed â perfectly false. When Winfrey made him watch a video of himself lying under oath, he appeared distant and halting. Later, he said he was embarrassed â but his expression suggested otherwise. She couldnât break through. Armstrong claimed he didnât feel he was cheating; he was leveling the playing field. It sounded like he was describing someone else. Even when acknowledging heâd been a bully, there was no hint of introspection. Maybe he doesnât have a soul to search. The interview â part one of two, with part two airing Friday â was a test for both. Armstrong hoped to earn enough public sympathy to salvage his ruined legacy. He failed. Winfrey aimed to reclaim some of her cultural prominence after leaving daytime TV for cable. She succeeded. He could have chosen '60 Minutes,' the 'Today' show, or 'Katie.' Instead, he chose Oprah. She remains the only host seen as capable of balancing toughness with empathy when confronting fallen stars â even when their transgressions far exceed typical celebrity missteps. David Zurawik, television critic for the Baltimore Sun, argues the media landscape has fractured, making it harder for TV to function as a unifying space for public confessions and redemption. Maybe heâs right. I donât forgive Lance Armstrong â he lied to me twice. And I suspect most of America wonât, either. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Howard Kurtz.

article_content: Thousands of passengers traveling to and from Gatwick Airport experienced significant disruptions after a Virgin Atlantic Boeing 747-400 made an emergency return shortly after takeoff due to a technical fault. The aircraft, carrying 447 passengers and 15 crew members bound for Las Vegas, developed a hydraulic issue that prevented one set of landing gear from deploying. After circling the airport to dump fuel, the plane landed safely with only three of its four landing gear units extended. The incident caused the airportâs single runway to close for approximately three hours, affecting nearly 10,000 travelers. Airlines including EasyJet and British Airways canceled dozens of flights and diverted others to nearby airports such as Bristol, Bournemouth, and Southampton. Despite the tension onboard, passengers reported the crew remained calm and informative throughout the ordeal. Many described the landing as 'textbook,' with some applauding the pilots upon touchdown. One passenger noted, 'We were told to brace for impact â then it was just smooth. Everyone breathed a sigh of relief.' Virgin Atlantic CEO Craig Kreeger confirmed all passengers and crew had safely disembarked and expressed deep appreciation for the crewâs professionalism. The airline announced a special flight the following day to transport all affected passengers to Las Vegas, assuring everyone would be accommodated. Gatwick Airport, the worldâs busiest single-runway airport, advised travelers to check airline updates via official channels and offered food, water, and assistance through staff and volunteers. Emergency services stood by during the landing, and engineers conducted a full inspection before the runway reopened at 7:03 p.m.

article_content: A year after Pakistan was hit by historic floods, the damage lingers far beyond the receded waters. More than 33 million people were directly impacted, with over 20 million needing emergency help. Nearly eight million were forced from their homes, and at least two million houses were destroyed. Even now, around 1.5 million people remain displaced. For many, food, clean water, and safe shelter are still out of reach â more than 40% depend entirely on aid to survive. While the most urgent crises have been partially managed, a quieter crisis is unfolding: deepening climate anxiety. Though the term is recent, the feeling isnât â communities have lived for years with the dread of recurring disasters. As floods become more common, families face endless cycles of loss, with no time to rebuild before the next one hits. People arenât just tired â theyâre terrified. Many have no plan if their homes, already barely standing, wash away again. And hereâs the cruelest part: Pakistan emits less than 1% of global greenhouse gases, yet itâs among the worldâs most vulnerable to climate chaos. Without meaningful global action, this anxiety will only grow â especially among those who did the least to cause it.

article_content: In October 2006, two teenage girlsâAmy Rademaker, 15, and Natasha Weigel, 17âdied when the Chevy Cobalt they were riding in crashed on a rural road in Wisconsin. The cause: a defective ignition switch that unexpectedly slipped into the 'accessory' position, shutting down power steering and airbags moments before impact. The driver, Megan Phillips, survived but sustained permanent brain injuries. General Motors had known about this dangerous flaw for over ten years and affected more than 2.6 million vehicles before finally recalling them in early 2014. Fearing that GM might invoke bankruptcy protections to shield itself in court, the families of Rademaker and Weigel opted to settle their lawsuit out of court. Margie Beskau, Amyâs mother, told CNBC: 'No amount of money brings my daughter back, but Iâm ready to move on.' She explained that settling provided both financial certainty and emotional peace, given the uncertainty of a trial outcome. GM has allocated up to $600 million in a compensation fund for victims. Federal investigations by Congress and the Justice Department continue, with reports confirming that both GM and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration ignored early warningsâincluding those from a Wisconsin state trooper who identified the ignition defect shortly after the crash.

article_content: A Norwegian man of Iranian-Kurdish descent, Zaniar Matapour, 44, has been formally charged with aggravated terrorism for a deadly shooting in Oslo on June 25, 2022. The attack, aimed at attendees of an LGBTQ+ festival, left two people dead and nine others critically injured, mostly near the popular gay bar, London Pub. According to prosecutor Sturla HenriksbÃ¸, Matapour unleashed 10 rounds from a machine gun and eight from a handgun into a crowd of around 560 people. He had previously sworn loyalty to the Islamic State, prosecutors say. The assault sent waves of fear through the city, prompting authorities to cancel the annual Pride parade due to security concerns. Matapour was apprehended immediately by bystanders and has refused to cooperate with investigators. Meanwhile, four other individuals remain under scrutiny; two are believed to be abroad, including a prominent Norwegian radical Islamist reportedly hiding in Pakistan. Authorities emphasize that while only Matapour has been charged, the probe into others remains active and serious. His trial, expected to last two months, begins in March. If convicted, he could face up to 30 years in prison. The incident has deeply shaken Norway â a country known for its peace and low crime â reminding citizens of past tragedies like the 2011 Utoya massacre and other recent lone-wolf attacks, including a 2021 knife-and-bow assault that claimed five lives.

article_content: Seven decades after vanishing in the brutal fighting on Saipan during World War II, U.S. Army Private Bernard Gavrin of Brooklyn will finally be laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery on September 12. His remains, unearthed last year by a Japanese nonprofit team digging through wartime debris in the Northern Mariana Islands, were positively identified using DNA from a living relative â a breakthrough that brought long-awaited closure to his family. Gavrin, just 29 when he went missing on July 7, 1944, was declared dead a year later, and by 1948, officials believed his body could never be recovered. But persistent efforts on Saipan â where intense battles claimed thousands â led to the discovery of multiple sets of remains, including his. Among the personal effects found with his bones were items that helped confirm his identity. His nephew, 82-year-old David Rogers of Florida, recalls vividly the last time he saw his uncle: as a young boy, wounded and in bed, Gavrin quietly entered his room, kissed his forehead, and woke him. That tender moment became one of his most cherished memories â made even more poignant by the telegram that shattered his grandmotherâs world when news arrived that Bernard was missing. âItâs unbelievable,â Rogers said. âTo bury him in Arlingtonâ¦ itâs the highest honor this country can give.â

(CNN) -- President Obama called income inequality 'the defining issue of our time' in his 2012 State of the Union address â though he never used the exact phrase. Perhaps thatâs because 'income inequality' is a term many have heard but few truly understand. Rather than overwhelming his audience with jargon, Obama anchored his message in the familiar ideal of the American Dream: 'the basic American promise,' as he put it, 'that if you work hard, you can do well enough to raise a family, own a home, send your kids to college, and save for retirement.' He added, 'The defining issue of our time is how to keep that promise alive. No challenge is more urgent. No debate is more important.'

But what exactly is income inequality, and why does it matter so much today?

Income inequality describes how evenly or unevenly income is distributed across a society. In the United States, income is highly concentrated among the wealthiest, creating a wide gap between the richest and poorest. By contrast, Scandinavian nations exhibit lower inequality due to broader distribution of prosperity.

Some economists argue that 'wealth inequality' â which includes assets like property and investments â paints a starker picture than income alone. Others use the broader term 'economic inequality.'

The most widely used measure is the Gini coefficient, which quantifies how far a nationâs income distribution deviates from perfect equality. A score of 0 means everyone earns the same; 100 means one person earns everything. According to the CIA World Factbook, the U.S. has a Gini coefficient of 45. Sweden, one of the most equal countries, scores 23. Lesotho in southern Africa leads the list with 63.2.

Other methods include comparing the income share of the top 20% versus the bottom 20%.

Since the late 1970s, income inequality in the U.S. has steadily widened. Experts cite factors including tax cuts for the wealthy, the expansion of the finance industry, and automation replacing middle-class jobs. Meanwhile, the richest Americans now earn a larger share of national income than at any point since the late 1920s.

Is more income inequality inherently bad? Few argue that everyone should earn identical incomes. But many economists and philosophers warn that extreme inequality harms society. Joseph Stiglitz says it's 'holding back' the economic recovery. Kate Pickett links it to higher rates of obesity, violence, and incarceration. Thomas Pogge warns it erodes social equality, fostering a 'Downton Abbey'-style class divide. Robert Reich likens the economy to a ladder: if the rungs are too far apart, upward mobility becomes nearly impossible.

Conservatives counter that inequality drives competition, innovation, and effort â essential for capitalism.

Interestingly, the U.S. ranks as more unequal than several nations most Americans would consider less developed â including Nigeria (Gini: 54.6), Uganda (44.1), Senegal (42.1), Nicaragua (44.3), and Mauritania (42.5). This reflects internal disparity, not absolute poverty. For example, Niger has low inequality simply because almost everyone is poor. Still, research suggests that extreme inequality â regardless of national wealth â weakens social trust and cohesion.

article_content: An Oregon woman was sentenced on Friday to serve 3 to 15 years in prison for abandoning the body of her 89-year-old mother outside a Michigan thrift store. 'I understand I need to be punished for my poor decisionsâthey were neither sensible nor logical,' Kelly Rhodes said before her sentencing in St. Clair County Circuit Court. The 49-year-old from Salem pleaded guilty in November to manslaughter, fourth-degree vulnerable adult abuse, and removing a body without authorization from a medical examiner. The body of Rhodesâ mother, Mary Grania, was found wrapped in blankets behind a Goodwill store near Port Huron in March 2013. Rhodes had planned to move to Canada with her mother and belongings, seeking to live with a former boyfriend after her husbandâs death, according to the Port Huron Times Herald. Mary Grania died in the vehicle shortly after the pair were denied entry into Ontario. Her remains were discovered on March 13, 2013, concealed beneath snow and blankets near a dumpster. Detectives determined the body had been there since at least March 3. An autopsy revealed no signs of trauma, but medical examiner Daniel Spitz noted that her deteriorating health may have been exacerbated by neglect. Judge Cynthia Lane stated that Rhodes could have sought helpâcontacting family or arranging professional careâbut instead made choices that were 'not right.' Defense attorney Sharon Parrish explained that Rhodes removed her mother from a nursing home three years earlier at her motherâs request, and later became overwhelmed by caregiving responsibilities after becoming a widow. Senior Assistant Prosecutor Mona Armstrong argued that Rhodesâ actions were 'shocking and cold,' emphasizing that her mother deserved basic dignity in her final days after raising her.

article_content: In the complex overlap of economics and politics, a new metric has emerged: trillion is the new billion. One trillion U.S. dollar bills stacked vertically would stretch nearly 68,000 miles â about 109,400 kilometers â reaching roughly a third of the way to the Moon. To put it simply: a billion is a thousand million; a trillion is a thousand billion. That means a trillion is a one followed by twelve zeros. Senator Mitch McConnell pointed out that Americans have grown numb to such massive figures. 'If you spent a million dollars every day since Jesus was born,' he said, 'you still wouldnât have spent a trillion.' Mathematician John Allen Paulos from Temple University confirmed that even McConnellâs analogy underestimates the scale: spending a million dollars daily for 2,000 years would total only three-quarters of a trillion. 'Itâs a big number no matter how you slice it,' Paulos said. Paulos offered another vivid comparison: a million seconds equals about 11.5 days; a billion seconds, roughly 32 years; a trillion seconds, an astonishing 32,000 years. 'Think of it like a jail sentence â would you rather serve 11.5 days, 32 years, or 32,000 years? People conflate them because they sound similar, but the difference is staggering.' With the U.S. national debt surpassing $10 trillion â and recent actions including a $700 billion bank bailout and an $800+ billion stimulus package â the sheer scale of money being discussed has become almost abstract. Paulos suggests reframing these numbers through familiar government budgets: the Environmental Protection Agencyâs annual budget is about $7.5 billion. A trillion dollars could fund it for over 130 years. The National Science Foundation or National Cancer Institute, each with budgets around $5â6 billion, could be funded for nearly two centuries. The contrast is striking. In 1993, President Clinton sought a $30 billion jobs package â and failed to secure it. Last year, President Bush signed a $168 billion stimulus â a figure that now seems modest. Todayâs proposals hover near $900 billion, with total financial interventions projected to exceed $7 trillion. Despite the enormity, the U.S. economy remains vast â its GDP stands at approximately $14 trillion. Yet questions linger: Can we truly afford this? Former Fed Chair Paul Volcker called the situation 'the mother of all crises.' As Paulos noted, the word 'number' might be better pronounced 'numb-er' â because when it comes to trillions, weâre not just dealing with numbers. Weâre dealing with something that feels beyond comprehension.

article_content: A new government-funded report by the Urban Institute reveals that a disproportionately high number of homeless LGBTQ youth in New York engage in survival sex to meet basic needs and stay alive. Over a three-year period, researchers interviewed 283 participants aged 15 to 21 (with a few older individuals). On average, respondents reported seeing 3 to 6 customers per day, with transactions ranging from $90 to $230. Approximately 90% said the work left them feeling frustrated, dirty, or endangered. Yet, more than 80% also noted positive aspectsâparticularly meeting essential needs and, in some cases, forming a sense of community. 'It's not as bad as sleeping under a bridge or going without food,' one participant said. Nearly half (46%) became involved through friends or peers; 26% were approached by strangers. Most found clients on the streets of New York or through online advertisements. Of the respondents, 47% identified as male, 36% as female, and 16% as transgender. About 90% were Black, Latino, or multiracial. Nearly 60% lived in shelters or on the streets, often after being expelled from home or aging out of foster care. One 19-year-old gay man shared that his mother forced him out because she rejected his sexuality: 'She didn't want me being gay. She wanted grandchildren. She didn't like my lifestyleâbut she still loved me.' Many participants carried protective items such as knives or Mace. During active periods, they averaged 11 to 18 transactions per week. The study, funded by the Justice Department's Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention, recommends tailored interventions: safe housing, accessible healthcare, and pathways to employmentâall designed with the specific needs of LGBTQ youth in mind. The Urban Institute did not estimate the total number of LGBTQ youth in NYCâs commercial sex market but cited prior research suggesting between 2,500 and 4,000 young people of all sexual orientations are affected. Lead author Meredith Dank concluded: 'They don't see themselves as victims... but it's not empowering for them to be doing this. These are kids in very desperate situations who will do what they need to do to survive.'

article_content: Their preparations for the World Cup have been meticulously planned by a dedicated team of sports scientists, physiotherapists, and nutritionists. It is therefore surprising that Englandâs footballers were allowed to enjoy a feast of burgers the night after returning to Rio following their opening-game loss. BBC sports presenter Gabby Logan revealed that Roy Hodgsonâs team dined at Aquarela Burger, a restaurant renowned for serving some of Rio de Janeiroâs best fast foodâincluding a massive 10oz 'Mega Burger'. In doing so, they inadvertently blocked Logan from sampling the Argentine beef patties herself, as the entire venue had been privately booked. The Football Association confirmed that the playersâ nutritionists granted special permission for the treat at Aquarela Burger, located within the five-star Royal Tulip Hotel, where the team is based in Rio. Of greater concern, a Brazilian consumer group had reported, a month prior, finding food well past its expiration date at the same hotel. Restaurant reviews indicate Aquarela Burger has long been popular with Brazilian teams Vasco da Gama and Flamengo and remains open until 1 a.m. daily. Hodgson maintains a more relaxed approach to diet than his predecessor Fabio Capello, having reinstated the use of tomato ketchup and brown sauce after they were previously banned. Logan, 41, who is also staying at the Royal Tulip, wrote on her blog about how the 'Three Lions' ruined her dinner plans on Monday night. She described eagerly anticipating the burgers after seeing ITV reporters enjoy them, comparing her craving to a dog watching a roast dinner. Upon approaching the restaurant, she found a 'Private Event â Closed' sign. Peering inside, she saw England players devouring the burgers. She ended up eating chicken soup next doorâthough she said she didnât resent them. A source close to the team told the Daily Mail: 'Poor Gabby missed a trickâshe couldâve ordered from the adjacent hotel restaurant. She just needed to check the menu.' An FA spokesperson added: 'The team received a special treat, approved by nutritionists. After more than a month together and burning thousands of calories, one burger posed no health risk.' Several rival teams have also been permitted comfort foods: Italy brought parmesan, olive oil, and prosciutto; the U.S. brought oatmeal, Cheerios, peanut butter, and A1 Steak Sauce; Mexico traveled with chili peppers, chipotle, and even cactus. Meanwhile, England striker Daniel Sturridge posted a candid selfie on Twitter expressing frustration after his hotel TV malfunctioned during an NBA game. The 24-year-old Liverpool forward shared two photosâone of himself in his England jersey, another of the blank screenâwith the caption: 'Just when I start getting into the game and itâs going off... Iâm fuming right now!!!' Brazil 2014 has become the first true 'selfie World Cup,' with players widely sharing personal moments on social media. Over 10,000 users have shared or favorited a photo of the England team traveling to their match against Italy. Itâs not just players: Iranian President Hassan Rouhani tweeted a selfie of himself watching Iranâs 0â0 draw with Nigeriaâwearing an Iranian football shirt and tracksuit instead of his usual clerical robes. He wrote: 'Proud of our boys who secured our first pointâhopefully the first of many more to come.' German Chancellor Angela Merkel also joined the trend, posing for a selfie with Germany and Arsenal striker Lukas Podolski after Germanyâs 4â0 win over Portugal. She had earlier been photographed in the changing room before players had fully dressed.

article_content: Just minutes before jury selection began in the trial of five former New Orleans police officers accused of shooting unarmed civilians after Hurricane Katrina, a scathing online comment appeared on the New Orleans Times-Picayuneâs website. 'NONE of these guys should have ever been given a badge,' wrote the user 'legacyusa.' 'We should research how they got on the police department, who trained them, who supervised them â and why were they ever promoted? You put crap in â you get crap out!!!' That commenter turned out to be Sal Perricone, one of the top federal prosecutors in New Orleans. His post was not an isolated incident. Multiple anonymous, hostile comments â made by at least three Justice Department officials using pseudonyms â helped create what Judge Kurt D. Engelhardt later described as a '21st century carnival atmosphere' that poisoned the 2011 trial. In a 129-page ruling, Engelhardt overturned the officersâ convictions on 25 counts of civil rights violations, citing 'egregious and inflammatory' prosecutorial misconduct. 'This case started as one featuring allegations of brazen abuse of authority, violation of the law and corruption of the criminal justice system; unfortunately, though the focus has switched from the accused to the accusers, it has continued to be about those very issues,' he wrote. Perricone, under multiple aliases, had been publicly denouncing the NOPD since at least 2008. Six months before the trial, he called the department 'a collection of self-centered, self-promoting, insular, arrogant, overweening, prevaricating, libidinous fools... the entire agency should be re-engineered from the ground up.' Another DOJ official, Jan Mann, also posted anonymously. Meanwhile, Karla Dobinski, a senior attorney on the DOJâs 'taint team' â tasked with ensuring immunity-granted testimony wasnât misused â posted six times during the trial praising pro-prosecution commenters. She claimed she was seeking insider information, but Engelhardt found her reasoning implausible, stating she 'fanned the flames' of public outrage. The five officers received prison sentences ranging from six to 65 years. Robert Faulcon received the longest term; Arthur Kaufman, the shortest. All were convicted in 2011 and sentenced in 2012. The Justice Department has since expressed disappointment in the ruling and is reviewing its options. Meanwhile, Perricone and Mann have left their positions since their roles were exposed in 2012. Dobinskiâs current status remains unclear. Engelhardt concluded: 'After much reflection, the court cannot journey as far as it has in this case only to ironically accept grotesque prosecutorial misconduct in the end.' The officers will now face a new trial.

article_content: Arranging pizza deliveries to strangers might sound like a prankâbut on Reddit, itâs become a powerful act of charity. Ashley Qualls, a resident of Santa Clarita, California, discovered this firsthand after posting on the popular link-sharing platform seeking ways to help those in need. A user suggested she explore 'Random Acts of Pizza,' a subreddit where people post urgent food requestsâand others fulfill them with delivered pies. Among the heartfelt messages: a man stranded away from home without his wallet, another without a credit card surviving on tortillas. But the true mission of Random Acts of Pizza, according to its founders and many members, is to assist those too vulnerable to feed themselvesâyet still tech-savvy enough to reach out online. Qualls has now sent 10 pizzas, each arriving within 30 minutes, often accompanied by grateful photos of empty boxes. She calls it 'instant gratification'âa stark contrast to slower charitable processes sheâs known. The subreddit has surged in popularity, drawing 226,000 visitors in a single week. Other Reddit-driven initiatives like SnackExchange, Food Pantry, and Closet Swap echo the same spirit of peer-to-peer giving. Even Redditâs small internal team was stunned by the movementâs growth. Earlier this month, they pooled $120 to buy pizzas for the Homeless Youth Alliance in San Francisco. 'We never imagined Reddit would become a pizza-delivery network,' said Erik Martin, Redditâs new general manager. Donors receive private addresses and order via popular delivery platforms. The concept was born from Daniel Rogers, a Texas lawyer, and John Mitchell, a former Idaho tech workerâboth unemployed during the economic downturn. 'Pizza was the one comfort food I couldnât afford,' Rogers explained. 'It wasnât about the pizza. It was about hope.' Rogers and Mitchellânever having met in personâare now trying to partner with national chains like Dominoâs and Little Caesars. While both companies have shown mild interest, no formal collaboration exists. Reddit has also reached out to restaurant partners, but responses remain limited. To expand access, the team requested CashStarâa payment processor used by many donorsâto enable international credit card donations. CashStarâs CEO reportedly had never heard of the group.
