article_content: A Texas animal shelter may face legal action after euthanizing a puppy last week, citing 'unknown demons' as the reason for its aggression. The New Braunfels Humane Societyâs decision to euthanize Baby George â an 11-week-old Dachshund-Chihuahua mix found abandoned in July â has been challenged by Elaine Buchhorn, who claims the dog was not aggressive and that she was never notified before the procedure. Buchhorn, who brought the puppy to the shelter with the intent of ensuring his safety around her two-year-old granddaughter and helping him find a new home, told the Houston Chronicle she repeatedly called to check on his status and explicitly requested to be contacted if adoption efforts failed. The shelter posted on its now-deleted Facebook page: 'The pup is now free, free from whatever unknown demons were causing the aggression.' Shelter executive director Billie Zercher stated that Baby George bit two staff members on separate occasions, triggering their policy to euthanize animals exhibiting aggression toward humans. Zercher emphasized that Buchhorn signed a release form transferring full legal rights to the shelter upon surrender, and that the facility receives thousands of animals annually â making individual notifications impractical. Buchhorn, deeply distressed, said she regrets bringing the dog to the shelter and has yet to receive an apology. She is considering legal action for alleged violations of animal care laws. One local resident has already filed a police complaint. The shelter confirmed that 500 of the 4,000 animals taken in this year were euthanized but declined to specify reasons.

article_content: In early March 2014, a young postal worker in Long Island sparked a community uproar when more than a thousand pieces of mail went missing â not due to service delays, but because someone had deliberately thrown them away. Patrick Paskett, 24, who had been working for the U.S. Postal Service since June 2013, was arrested after residents in Seaford and Massapequa Park reported not receiving vital deliveries, including checks and utility bills. Federal investigators, acting on tips, tracked Paskettâs movements on March 6 and discovered him disposing of stamped mail at four separate trash sites. He later confessed to doing this roughly 15 times over the previous three months. Authorities recovered 1,018 items, including letters and packages, from the locations he showed them. In a statement to the court, Paskett admitted he knew destroying mail was wrong. Though still technically employed by USPS until legal proceedings conclude, he has been suspended from delivering mail. Paskett was released without bail but now faces up to five years in prison if convicted. One local resident, Christine Augello, summed up the frustration: 'People are waiting for their checks... he should have never done that.' His court date remains unconfirmed, and he continues to live with his parents while awaiting trial.

article_content: In a shocking act of violence tied to a local building dispute, Michael Martin John O'Connell, a 50-year-old man from Middleton, South Australia, brutally killed six young miniature horses in December. The horses â two colts and four fillies, all around two years old â had their throats slit at a stable in Clayton Bay, roughly 70 kilometers south of Adelaide. Julie Jackson, the owner of the stud, described the scene as devastating, calling O'Connell 'a very, very dangerous man.' She and her husband have since sold the property and moved away, unable to return to the site of the trauma. On Tuesday, O'Connell pleaded guilty to trespassing â a charge that was upgraded because prosecutors argued he entered the property with the intent to destroy property valued at over $30,000 and used a deadly weapon. In exchange, six separate charges of animal cruelty were dropped, as the property damage charge carries a more severe potential sentence under South Australian law. Terry Hocking, the horsesâ trainer, recounted finding the first horse he loved with its throat cut, then discovering five more in similar condition. He described three surviving horses as deeply traumatized, requiring long-term care to recover emotionally. Outside the Adelaide Magistrates Court, Jackson, surrounded by family and supporters, expressed her desire for O'Connell to serve jail time. She added that the case has sparked an outpouring of global solidarity, with messages of support flooding in from across the world. The matter has been referred to the District Court for sentencing on July 21, where O'Connell could face significant prison time due to the aggravated nature of the trespassing charge.

article_content: Peter Clague, the newly appointed headmaster of Bromsgrove School in Worcestershire, has denied allegations that he assaulted his ex-wife, Jeanne Jackman. Clague, 48, is set to begin his role at the prestigious UK boarding school on September 1, following his tenure in New Zealand. In September 2010, Jackman alleges that Clague ran at her, shook her by the shoulders, and pushed her down a flight of stairs at their former home in Greenhithe, Auckland, resulting in a fractured tailbone. She did not report the incident to police until more than two years later, which under New Zealand law prevented criminal chargesâonly a formal warning was issued. Jackman publicly criticized the policeâs decision at the time, stating: 'I believe this makes a mockery of calls to address domestic violence. Either we take the issue of domestic violence seriously in New Zealand, or we donât.' She subsequently launched a private prosecution against Clague, who has pleaded not guilty. Jackman also claims Clague subjected her to prolonged psychological abuse. Clague disputes the claims, asserting they are false and motivated by resentment following their breakup. He previously stated: 'My career is on the whim of a woman who is angry over a break-up. Principals donât come back from false allegations like this.' Bromsgrove School, which charges Â£31,000 annually and educates 1,260 students aged 2â18, has publicly backed Clague. Its Chairman of Governors, Stewart Towe, affirmed: 'The governors are wholly satisfied with the integrity of Peter Clague and followed due diligence in the appointment process.' Philippa Fee, Chair of Kristin School in Auckland, praised Clagueâs leadership, noting his pivotal role in fostering a positive school culture. Founded in the 1560s, Bromsgrove counts among its alumni actor Trevor Eve, poet A.E. Housman, musician John Ilsley, and former CBI head Lord Digby Jones.

What began as a routine walk took an unexpected turn when Tessa began digging near some shoreline debris. After a quick look, he recognized it as a human leg bone. As they examined the area, Tessa continued to dig, revealing another fragment â this time, the lower portion of a leg, still wearing a sock. Barrett noted the sock appeared to fit a manâs foot, though he emphasized it was only an observation. Later, police arrived with trained cadaver dogs and uncovered additional human remains. By Sunday, officials confirmed all the bones were human. The beach has since been closed as forensic teams work to process the scene. The Essex County District Attorneyâs office is now reviewing missing persons reports in hopes of identifying the individual(s) behind the remains.

article_content: A five-year-old boy named Noah Ritter from Pottstown, Pennsylvania, turned into an overnight internet star after a TV interview went viral â not because of anything extraordinary he did, but because he kept saying the word 'apparently.' In a now-famous clip from the Wayne County Fair, Noah answered questions about a new ride with the word 'apparently' repeated eight times in under a minute, while also insisting, multiple times, that heâd never been on live TV before. What made it even funnier? He didnât actually know what the word meant. Fast forward a few weeks: Noahâs charm landed him a spot in a commercial for Freshpet, a company that sells refrigerated pet food. In the ad, heâs seen playing with puppies, grinning at the camera, and delivering lines like, 'Apparently Freshpet food is the best food than ordinary dog food,' with perfect toddler confidence. He even invites viewers to call him directly â and gives out his phone number. The commercial feels spontaneous, almost like a kid just being himself, which is probably why it works so well. After his initial fame, Noah appeared on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, where he calmly told the host he now prefers the word 'seriously.' When asked if he knew what 'apparently' meant, he shrugged and said, 'I donât know how to spell it, and I donât know what it means â I just say it when somethingâs annoying.' His innocence and lack of self-awareness turned a simple linguistic habit into a global moment of joy. Though the commercial is clearly marketing, it doesnât feel forced. It leans into Noahâs natural quirks rather than scripting them away. And honestly? Thatâs what made people fall in love with him in the first place.

article_content: A New Jersey appellate court has ruled that a judgeâs order prohibiting a mother from posting about her children or ex-husband on Facebook did not violate her constitutional rights. The restriction was imposed in 2011 as a condition of her probation following her attempt to kidnap her two children and take them to Canada, in violation of a custody agreement. Prosecutors and the ex-husbandâs family had argued that her Facebook postsâfilled with references to serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, the Book of Revelation, Satan, and Adolf Hitlerâwere threatening and psychologically harmful. The judge explicitly told her: 'You can talk about what you want, but donât mention your husband or the children. Thatâs off limits.' In 2012, the mother resumed posting under the coded term 'Camelot' to refer to her family. The court determined this violated her probation terms. She appealed, claiming the order was unconstitutionally vague and infringed on her First Amendment rights. The appellate panel rejected her argument, concluding the restriction was narrowly tailored to promote her rehabilitation and protect her children. The court emphasized that the order did not ban all speech, only speech targeting specific individuals. The woman, who has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was arrested in May 2011. She later pleaded guilty to interference with custody; the more serious kidnapping charge was dropped. To protect the privacy of her children, her identity was withheld in court records.

article_content: Shivering and terrified, five 12-week-old English Bull Terrier-cross puppies were abandoned beside a busy road near the Battersea Dogs & Cats Home in Old Windsor, Berkshire, on New Yearâs Eve. Found inside a small plastic box with no food or water and covered in dirt, the puppies had clearly been deliberately left behind. Staff at the rescue center believe the puppies were bred specifically as Christmas gifts but failed to sell in time, prompting their cruel disposal. Centre Manager Kaye Mughal said, 'Given the timing, weâre concerned they were bred for profit â and discarded when they didnât turn a quick buck.' Thankfully, the puppies were discovered just hours before midnight. In honor of the occasion, staff named them Midnight, Big Ben, Chimes, Bubbles, and Fizz. They were immediately warmed, fed, hydrated, and cleaned. The puppies were extremely distressed, having been confined in the cramped box. Their coats were matted, and they were desperate to escape. Battersea reported a surge in abandoned animals over the holidays: between 24 December and 1 January, its three centers took in 96 dogs and 52 cats â including 36 dogs and 11 cats at the Old Windsor site alone. Many were strays, some intentionally dumped. Mughal emphasized: 'People often buy pets as Christmas presents, only to realize weeks later theyâre too much work. By March, the novelty wears off â and so does responsibility.' She urged the public: 'Please choose toys or chocolates over living creatures. These puppiesâ story is a heartbreaking reminder of what happens when animals are treated as disposable items.' All five puppies are now recovering and will remain at the center for at least seven days before being available for adoption. Mughal described them as lively and affectionate: 'Fizz is bold and loves attention; Big Ben is her fearless brother; Chimes is sensitive; Bubbles is shy and clings to Midnight, whoâs the gentlest of them all.' 'Theyâve had a terrible start,' she added, 'but 2013 will be the year they finally find love.' To adopt one of the puppies or any other animal from Battersea Old Windsor, contact 01784 494443 or bow.rehomers@battersea.org.uk.

article_content: Nearly two decades after the Srebrenica massacre claimed the lives of thousands of Bosniak men and boys, a former Bosnian Serb intelligence chief has been sentenced to life in prison for his role in the atrocities. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), based in The Hague, found Zdravko Tolimir guilty of genocide, conspiracy to commit genocide, and other crimes linked to the 1995 fall of Srebrenica â an event widely recognized as the worst massacre in Europe since World War II. The killings, part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing, targeted Bosniak males under the direction of ultra-nationalist Serb forces seeking to ethnically homogenize the region. According to the United Nations, between 6,000 and 8,000 men and boys were systematically murdered. The tribunal concluded that the physical and psychological harm inflicted constituted clear acts of genocide. Tolimirâs case was one of 12 major prosecutions handled by the ICTY, which has indicted 161 individuals for grave violations of international humanitarian law between 1991 and 2001. He was a key subordinate to Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military commander arrested in Serbia in 2011 and now also standing trial for genocide in The Hague. The Bosnian War, which lasted from 1992 to 1995, left more than 100,000 people dead and forced nearly two million from their homes.

article_content: On Monday, Facebook unveiled an update to Graph Search that lets users search for specific conversation topics within status updates, comments, and posts. Now, users can look up phrases like 'posts about Breaking Bad' or simply 'Breaking Bad' to find relevant discussions. The enhanced feature also allows filtering by time and location â for instance, 'posts by my friends from last month' â or identifying content the user themselves created or commented on. This upgrade makes Facebook a more dynamic space for real-time dialogue, a key area where the platform is striving to rival Twitter. Both platforms are locked in a battle for attention during major live TV events such as the Emmys, NFL Monday Night Football, and the finale of Breaking Bad. While viewers watch TV, Facebook and Twitter aim to capture their reactions and opinions in real time. With Graph Search, users can now instantly access ongoing conversations about a show or game â even if those posts donât appear at the top of their News Feed. Unlike Twitter, Facebook allows users to revisit and explore past discussions hours or even days after an event. To fuel these conversations, Facebook has been forging partnerships with media outlets. Earlier this month, it struck a deal with FOX Sports to display live Facebook data and user comments alongside NFL and college football broadcasts. Other enhancements, including searchable hashtags and verified accounts, further improve topic discovery. According to Facebookâs Q2 earnings report, between 88 and 100 million users are active on the platform during primetime TV hours â a figure that advertisers are closely monitoring. Meanwhile, Twitter is preparing for its upcoming IPO, with reports suggesting filing documents imminently. Last week, Twitter announced advertising partnerships with CBS and the NFL to integrate live video directly into usersâ feeds. Facebookâs new Graph Search functionality is not yet available to all users. It began rolling out Monday to a limited test group and will expand gradually. Importantly, users can only search content that is either public or shared with them â private conversations remain protected unless explicitly made public. article_content: On Sunday evening, a gold-colored hatchback crashed through the front wall of a home in Blaenymaes, South Wales, startling three teenagers who were watching TV inside. Miraculously, none were injured. Stevie Jones, 17, Kieron Chapman, 16, and Michael Cuttle, 16, were unharmed as emergency crews arrived shortly after 8:20 p.m. The homeâs occupant, 57-year-old Diane Edwards, was visiting her son when she received a frantic call from her daughterââThereâs either a car in the garden or in the house.â She rushed home to find the vehicle embedded in the living room wall. The property, which sheâs lived in for 35 years, sustained visible damage but was declared structurally sound by authorities. Around 150 neighbors gathered to witness the aftermath. Two men from Swansea were later arrested: a 22-year-old suspected of driving under the influence, and a 24-year-old accused of fleeing the scene. Local councillor Terry Hennegan, whose home is nearby, called it the first major crash of its kind in nearly five years. He recalled past issues with speeding in the neighborhood but credited community and police efforts for reducing the problem. Swansea Council, which owns the property, confirmed inspectors have assessed the building and arranged urgent repairs. They also offered support to the tenant. Hennegan praised the family for their long-standing contributions to the community.

article_content: A Welsh politician is urging Oxford University to return the 'Red Lady of Paviland' â a 33,000-year-old skeleton discovered in Wales â to its place of origin. The remains, found in Goatâs Hole Cave on the Gower Peninsula in 1823 by an Oxford geology professor, are the oldest known ceremonial burial in Western Europe. Despite its name, the skeleton is that of a man, mistakenly identified as female due to decorative artifacts found nearby. The red coloration comes from ochre used in ancient burial rites. Currently held by Oxford University, the original bones are stored securely and not publicly displayed. However, a high-quality cast is permanently exhibited at the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, with another cast having been displayed at Londonâs Natural History Museum in 2014. Byron Davies, Assembly Member for South Wales, argues the skeleton rightfully belongs in Wales. He believes its return would strengthen regional identity and boost tourism in Gower and Swansea, where he proposes housing the remains in the Swansea Museum. Davies notes that Oxford previously loaned the bones to the National Museum and Galleries of Wales in 2009 and says he intends to initiate diplomatic talks with the university. He is also exploring funding options to ensure the skeletonâs safe preservation in Swansea. UK Culture Secretary Maria Miller, who grew up in Bridgend, has expressed support for returning the remains to Wales. Oxford University maintains that no formal repatriation request has been submitted. It emphasizes that any decision on repatriation requires review by the University Council, guided by curatorial expertise and institutional policy. Until such a request is made, the matter remains under consideration only in principle.

article_content: Illinois State Representative Keith Farnham, 66, has been charged with possessing and distributing child pornography using both state-issued and personal computers. The allegations include explicit online communications in which he reportedly described sexually abusing a six-year-old girl and expressed preference for children aged six to eight. Farnham, a Democrat who twice sponsored legislation to increase penalties for child sexual abuse, resigned on March 19, citing health concerns. His resignation came one week after federal authorities raided his Elgin home and state office. According to a sworn affidavit, investigators traced illegal images and videos â including footage of a six-month-old infant being abused â to a Yahoo email account linked to Farnham. Some files were sent from his state office computer, marked 'Property of the State of Illinois House of Representatives.' Online chats connected to his account allegedly contained graphic discussions with multiple users, including an undercover Homeland Security agent who received abusive material via email. Farnham is not currently charged in connection with the specific act of molesting the child mentioned in the chats, though the evidence remains central to the case. The investigation began after an anonymous tip led authorities to uncover hundreds of illicit files exchanged between August 2013 and January 2024. Farnham has not publicly commented on the charges and is scheduled to appear in court.

article_content: Thereâs something deeply healing about hitting the open road alone. My two-week journey from Seattle to Sacramentoâspanning over 2,200 milesâreconnected me with what truly matters: quiet moments, raw nature, and the courage to be by myself. Along the way, I wandered through the misty Hoh Rain Forest in Olympic National Park, where moss-draped trees older than Columbus stood silent and grand. The scent of damp earth and the hush of falling rain felt like a balm to my overstimulated mind. I stumbled upon Ruby Beach during a sudden downpourâand found myself utterly alone on the shore, waves crashing, wind whipping, the world reduced to just me and the Pacific. Later, after days of soggy camping and an accidental encounter with a banana slug the size of a loaf of bread, I treated myself to Sol Duc Hot Springs. Stepping into the mineral-rich waters, surrounded by evergreens, I finally let go. The heat seeped into my bones, and for the first time in months, I breathed easy. In Oregon, I descended into the limestone labyrinth of Oregon Caves, where guides shared tales of bears chased by dogs and couples marrying underground in faux caveman costumes. At 44 degrees inside, I clutched my jacket tightâbut the wonder outweighed the chill. In Mendocino, I ate an avocado sandwich perched on coastal rocks as the sun dipped low, salt spray kissing my skin. No itinerary had led me there, yet it became one of the tripâs most vivid memories. And then came the sequoias. In Calaveras Big Trees State Park, I stood beneath giants that had watched empires rise and fall. One tree, nearly 250 feet tall and wider than a bus, made me feel like a speck in time. My friendâs A-frame home nestled in Stanislaus National Forestâsurrounded not by neighbors, but by ancient pines and crystal riversâmade me envy a life lived in harmony with wild places. This trip taught me that being alone doesnât mean being lonely. It means listeningâto the wind, to your thoughts, to the quiet voice you usually drown out. Society tells us solitude is strange. But hereâs the truth: sometimes, the best companion youâll ever haveâ¦ is yourself.

article_content: Last Wednesday night, 44-year-old Terry Burns, a heart patient whoâd undergone a double bypass three years earlier, arrived at Royal Preston Hospital for routine tests. What should have been a short visit turned into a harrowing 12-hour wait â spent sitting upright in a plastic chair in the emergency departmentâs waiting area. His sister, Tina Burns-Moore, left him there in the evening, assuming heâd be moved to a bed once tests began. When she returned the next morning, he was still there â fully dressed, unwashed, and exhausted. No bed had been made available. Tina described the scene as chaotic: people moving in and out, a woman on a trolley being told to get up so the equipment could be reused. 'He came here for help,' she said. 'If you couldnât give him a bed, at least call us. We couldâve taken him home.' The hospital later apologized, acknowledging the delay in finding him a space. Though officials insisted thereâs no ongoing bed shortage, they admitted the facility had been overwhelmed by an unusually high number of patients that night. Terry eventually got a bed later the same day and was able to rest while awaiting results. The NHS Trust has launched an internal review to prevent similar incidents.

article_content: The operator of the crippled Fukushima nuclear plant has stated that it requires international assistance to stabilize and safely decommission the damaged reactors. This comes as regulators prepare to classify a new toxic water leak at Fukushima as a Level 3 'serious incident' â the most severe rating since the 2011 earthquake and tsunami triggered meltdowns in three reactors. Zengo Aizawa, Vice President of Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO), told reporters at a press conference on Wednesday evening that 'many countries outside Japan have experience decommissioning reactors, and we hope to consult them more and apply their knowledge. In that sense, we need support â not only from the Japanese government but from the international community.' Earlier that day, Japanâs Nuclear Regulation Authority (NRA) confirmed it expects to assign the leak a Level 3 rating on the International Nuclear and Radiological Event Scale (INES), pending input from the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). The IAEA has requested additional details about the leaking tankâs design and original purpose. 'The current situation has reached a point where increased surveillance alone cannot prevent further accidents,' said Shunichi Tanaka, Chairman of the NRA, during a news briefing. 'Our priority now is to reduce the risk of these incidents becoming catastrophic.' The leak, previously rated Level 1 ('anomaly'), involves approximately 300 tons of highly contaminated water. TEPCO reported that it has successfully transferred the radioactive water from the compromised tank â which holds up to 1,000 tons â to another storage unit. The IAEA acknowledged awareness of the planned classification and reiterated its readiness to assist upon request. Scientists have documented elevated radiation levels in seawater near the plant for over a year, pointing to persistent containment failures. In July, TEPCO admitted radioactive groundwater was seeping into the Pacific Ocean despite the installation of an underground ice wall intended to block such leaks â highlighting deepening concerns at the site. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has instructed his administration to pursue 'multiple, speedy, and sure' solutions to halt the spread of contaminated water, stating, 'We must address this at a national level.' Nuclear engineer Michael Friedlander, a former U.S. plant operator, agreed that a Level 3 classification was appropriate given the circumstances, but emphasized that public risk remains very low. 'This water is extremely radioactive â a grave hazard to workers handling it,' he told CNN. 'We still donât know precisely where the leak originates.' TEPCO spokesperson Mayumi Yoshida countered Friedlanderâs assessment, asserting that workers are adequately protected by specialized gear. Meanwhile, experts warn that technical and political barriers make any long-term solution exceptionally challenging.

article_content: Caste, or varna, is not a divine inventionâit was constructed by privileged groups to secure their own advantages. Though often associated with India, caste systems are not unique to it, nor should any nation be confined to a single social hierarchy. In Pakistan, caste may not be overt, but it quietly shapes many of the countryâs deepest social and economic challenges. Hindus make up roughly 1.2% of Pakistanâs population, and a significant number belong to Scheduled Castes. Under a 1957 presidential ordinance, 32 of Pakistanâs approximately 40 distinct castes were officially recognized as Scheduled Castesâmost linked to Hindu communities and shaped by historical upper-caste dominance. Discrimination against Dalits is most acute in rural regions, where low literacy rates and limited awareness of human rights enable exploitation. Local feudal landlords and segments of the rural upper-caste Hindu population perpetuate these abuses. The roots of caste-based exclusion stretch back centuries, predating Pakistanâs creation. Although constitutional and legal safeguards exist for minorities, enforcement remains weak. The story of Basanti Meghwarâs family is emblematic: for over two decades, they have been trapped in bonded labor, working in brick kilns to repay a debt taken to cover a hospital billâwith no formal documents to prove their plight. Civil society organizations like SPARC have intervened to free bonded laborers. Pannu Fair, who spent his childhood in servitude, was liberated and had his debt erased through a court ruling supported by SPARC. Dalits are disproportionately affected by bonded labor due to poverty, caste identity, and religious minority statusâall factors that compound their marginalization. Even if the severity of discrimination here is less visible than elsewhere, its consequences are profound: restricted access to education, employment, and political participation, including suppression of voting rights and barriers to running for office. Forced conversions further expose the vulnerability of marginalized communities. Yet, despite systemic barriers, some Dalits have risen to prominence. Sono Khangharani, with over 30 years in microfinance and development, has built institutions empowering marginalized groups. Krishna Kohliâonce a child laborer in a poor villageâbecame the first Hindu Dalit woman elected to Pakistanâs Senate, representing Nagarparkar in Sindh. Her journey embodies resilience. Activists like Radha Bheel, CEO of RADHA and Chair of Dalit Sujag Tehreek, highlight the lack of political voice and economic disparity among Dalits. Pushpa Kumari underscores how gender, caste, and religion intertwine to deepen oppression. Pirbhu Satyani, a Sindh-based advocate, calls attention to the silence surrounding caste discrimination in Punjab. The Government of Pakistan, especially in Sindh, has enacted laws and programs to protect minoritiesâbut implementation lags. Dalits seek not just protection, but transformation: dismantling systems that profit from exclusion. Only then can true security and dignity be secured for all. It is important to note that while the term 'Dalit' is widely used by activists in Pakistan, some communities prefer local terms like 'Achhoot' or 'Adim Jati'. Furthermore, caste-like social hierarchies exist within Muslim communities tooâincluding among groups like Bheels, Meghwars, and Chamarsâwho face similar marginalization, though rarely acknowledged in public discourse. Shahid is a Senior Research Analyst at the South Asia Research Institute for Minorities (SARIM), and Bheel is a Research Associate at SARIM.

article_content: After a 10-day preview for tech-savvy users, YouTube has officially launched its major redesign to everyone worldwide â rolling it out simultaneously at 4:30 p.m. ET on Thursday. Unlike Google, which typically phases in updates gradually, YouTube made a bold, global switch. At the heart of this overhaul is a new focus on channels. YouTube now sees itself less as a video repository and more as a modern cable TV platform â hosting millions of channels instead of just hundreds. To help users navigate this shift, a new 'Add Channels' button appears in the top-left corner, followed by a personalized section displaying your top 10 favorite channels, which you can pin for quick access. Margaret Stewart, Director of User Experience at YouTubeâs San Bruno headquarters, explains: 'The future of the YouTube experience has channels at the center. Itâs a container for all the worldâs video â and it needs to be the best home for that.' Visually, the platform has been refreshed: the YouTube logoâs colors have been subtly softened, and a light gray background now frames video content. These tweaks reflect closer alignment with Googleâs broader visual identity â a sign of deeper integration between the two teams, with increased collaboration between San Bruno and the Googleplex in Mountain View. The redesign also strengthens ties with Google+, while simultaneously simplifying sharing to Facebook and Twitter. Across devices, the update extends to YouTube apps â including Xbox â making channel browsing far more intuitive. For creators, YouTube introduces four new channel templates. Two stand out: one tailored for media networks (highlighting featured content), and another optimized for bloggers (showing latest uploads first). Executives stress this is just the beginning. article_content: In an indication of back-channel talks following the diplomatic row between Delhi and Ottawa after Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau alleged a potential link between the Indian government and the killing of Khalistani separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar, Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Canadian Foreign Minister Melanie Joly met last month in Washington, D.C., according to the UK-based Financial Times. While India did not officially confirm the meeting, the FT reported that 'Joly held a secret meeting with Indiaâs foreign minister, S. Jaishankar, in Washington,' citing people familiar with the situation. The report added that Ottawa was seeking to de-escalate tensions with New Delhi, which had warned that diplomats remaining beyond a specified deadline would lose diplomatic immunity. Several sources confirmed that Canada had not withdrawn any diplomats before the deadline. India had requested Ottawa to reduce its diplomatic staff by approximately 40 to achieve parity with Indiaâs diplomatic presence in Canada. India maintains about 20 diplomats in Canada, while Canada, according to sources, has roughly 60 â three times as many. Jaishankar was in Washington, D.C., during the last week of September, where he met with U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken and National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan. He confirmed that the Canada issue was raised in those discussions. Blinken urged India to 'cooperate fully' with Canadaâs ongoing investigation into Nijjarâs killing. Speaking at the Hudson Institute, Jaishankar said: 'To your question... Yes, I did discuss this with Jake Sullivan and Tony Blinken. They shared U.S. views and assessments on this whole situation, and I explained at length my governmentâs concerns. I think we both came out better informed.' On the state of India-Canada relations, Jaishankar noted that Trudeau initially raised the allegations privately, then publicly. 'Our response, both in private and public, was that his allegation is inconsistent with our policy. If your government has any specific, relevant information, we are open to examining it,' he said. 'Thatâs where the conversation stands at this point.' It is plausible that Jaishankar and Joly met in Washington, though no U.S. official acknowledged the encounter. Washington emerged as a key intermediary, given Canadaâs close alliance with the U.S. and Indiaâs growing strategic partnership with Washington. In early October, Joly stated that Canada would continue engaging with India privately. 'We believe in a strong diplomatic footprint in India,' she told reporters. 'We take the safety of our diplomats very seriously. Diplomatic conversations are most effective when kept private â especially during times of heightened tension.' Since the dispute began, at least five senior U.S. officials â Blinken, Sullivan, NSC Strategic Communications Coordinator John Kirby, U.S. Ambassador to India Eric Garcetti, and U.S. Ambassador to Canada David Cohen â have issued measured public statements, urging India to cooperate while cautioning Canada against premature escalation. India has dismissed Canadaâs claims as 'absurd' and 'politically motivated,' accusing Ottawa of failing to act against Khalistani elements within Canada and of providing no specific evidence regarding Nijjarâs killing. Yet, it has maintained an opening for dialogue, stating it would review any credible, specific information provided by Canada.

article_content: Francois Crepeau, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Migrant Rights, has ignited controversy after describing hostile attitudes toward migrants in the UK as 'utter bull****' â rooted in a fantasy of preserving a 2,000-year-old British culture. In an interview with the i newspaper, the Canadian expert rejected the notion that modern Britain must defend an ancient cultural identity against incoming migrants, calling such views dangerous myths. He further criticized the UK governmentâs decision to withdraw from Mediterranean search-and-rescue operations, stating that doing so effectively means allowing people to drown. Crepeau praised the multicultural openness of Tony Blairâs New Labour era, contrasting it with what he described as the exclusionary politics of UKIP. His remarks drew sharp rebukes from British politicians. Tory MP Dominic Raab accused him of 'offensive bigotry,' while UKIP leader Nigel Farage dismissed his comments as 'utter baloney,' arguing that Britain remains one of Europeâs most tolerant countries on immigration â though his claim comparing current migration to levels since 1066 is historically misleading. The controversy echoes broader tensions between the UN and UK authorities, following previous critiques by UN officials on housing policy, gender equality, and human rights â including controversial statements by Raquel Rolnik and Rashida Manjoo. The UK government maintains that it will prioritize public opinion over what it calls the 'unelected and unrealistic' pronouncements of international bureaucrats. He constantly sought the ball, even in tight spaces, rarely wasted a pass, cherished possession, and created chances. He scored, tracked back diligently, and worked tirelessly. He was, quite simply, head and shoulders above everyone else on the pitch. It was a joy to watch. 'Heâs making players around him better,' Cameron told me. 'Heâs getting comfortable. Heâs going to be known as our main guy â the one who makes us tick.' The club has had some extraordinary names â legends like Gordon Banks, Sir Stanley Matthews, Peter Shilton, and Sir Geoff Hurst. Others remain deeply beloved by fans: Mike Pejic, Terry Conroy, George Eastham, and Denis Smith, who all played pivotal roles in Stokeâs only major trophy win â the 1972 League Cup, a 2â1 victory over Chelsea at Wembley. But the 1972 Wembley victory over Chelsea remains their defining moment. At 24, Bojan has time to cement his legacy. But heâs also young enough to attract interest from top European clubs and reestablish himself on the global stage. article_content: Venue: Circuit of the Americas, Austin Circuit length: 5.513 km (3.425 miles) Laps: 56 Race distance: 308.405 km (191.111 miles) Lap record: 1:39.347 by Sebastian Vettel (2012) Number of corners: 20 (11 left-hand, 9 right-hand) Tyre compounds: Soft and Medium Track condition: Smooth Best overtaking opportunities: Turns 1 and 16 The next race on the Formula 1 calendar â the third-to-last of the season â will be the United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas in Austin. Lewis Hamilton celebrated on the podium in Austin after winning the 2012 race. Each of the 56 laps covers 5.513 km (3.425 miles), totaling 308.405 km (191.111 miles). Lewis Hamilton can set a new British record with his 32nd career Formula 1 victory, as he is currently tied with Nigel Mansell at 31 wins. Hamilton has won nine races this season. Only Michael Schumacher (11 in 2004) and Sebastian Vettel (13 in 2013) have won more in a single campaign. This season, Hamilton has won four races in a row on two separate occasions. Only Schumacher has matched this feat, achieving seven and then five consecutive wins in 2004. No driver has ever lost a World Championship after winning four consecutive Grands Prix â this has occurred 19 times before. Hamiltonâs win in Russia marked his 67th career podium, moving him ahead of Sebastian Vettel and one behind Rubens Barrichello in sixth place on the all-time list. With Nico Rosberg finishing second in Russia, Mercedes has secured nine one-two finishes this season â one shy of McLarenâs 1988 record of 10, set by Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost. Sebastian Vettel holds the current lap record at Circuit of the Americas with a time of 1:39.347. Lewis Hamilton collected his trophy from Vladimir Putin after winning the previous Grand Prix in Sochi, Russia. The Marussia F1 team has entered administration and will not compete in the United States Grand Prix. Mercedes could equal Red Bullâs 2011 record of 18 pole positions this season; they currently have 15 from 16 races. Mercedes may even break the all-time record for most wins in a single season. The current record of 15 is jointly held by Ferrari (2002, 2004) and McLaren (1988). Mercedes has 13 wins with three races remaining. With Caterham and Marussia in administration and absent this weekend, only 18 cars will line up on the grid â the fewest since the 2005 Monaco Grand Prix. The Circuit of the Americas is one of only four anti-clockwise circuits on the 2023 calendar, alongside Singapore, Interlagos, and Abu Dhabi. Austin is the 10th venue to host the United States Grand Prix. Previous hosts include Riverside, Sebring, Watkins Glen, Dallas, Detroit, Las Vegas, Long Beach, Phoenix, and Indianapolis.

article_content: Just days before what should have been the pinnacle of his basketball career â being selected in the NBA draft â Isaiah Austin received devastating news: a rare genetic condition called Marfan syndrome meant he could no longer compete at a high level. The 7-foot-1 center from Texas, once poised to become the NBAâs first partially blind player due to a past retinal detachment, learned that his heart and major arteries were dangerously enlarged. Any intense physical strain could lead to a fatal rupture. Though heartbreaking, doctors emphasized that catching this early might have saved his life. Marfan syndrome, caused by a faulty gene, weakens the bodyâs connective tissues. It often leads to unusually tall, slender builds, elongated limbs, and vision problems â all traits Austin displayed. But the real danger lies beneath the surface: weakened sections of the aorta, the main artery carrying blood from the heart, can tear without warning. Heart valve leaks and spinal curvatures are also common. Without diagnosis, these hidden risks can turn a routine game into a tragedy â as happened in 1986 with Olympic volleyball star Flo Hyman, who collapsed and died on the bench, unaware her aortic wall was already compromised. Today, around 200,000 Americans live with Marfan or a related disorder, nearly half without knowing it. While thereâs no cure, proper monitoring, medication, and sometimes surgery can allow individuals to live full, healthy lives. Experts stress that avoiding high-intensity sports is critical. For Austin, this diagnosis isnât just the end of a dream â itâs the beginning of a safer future.

article_content: Ronny Deila branded Craig Gordon 'fantastic' after the Celtic goalkeeper delivered a top-drawer performance to secure a 2-2 Europa League draw away at Salzburg. The Scottish champions took the lead twiceâfirst through debutant Wakaso Mubarak and later via a deflected effort from Scott Brown. Salzburg equalized twice: Alan levelled after Mubarakâs opener with a deflection off Efe Ambrose, and captain Jonathan Soriano equalized with a blistering free-kick 12 minutes from time. But for Gordonâs sublime fingertip save in the first half and a stunning double save in the second, Salzburg would likely have won. 'Craigâs performance was just marvellous,' said Deila, noting how the Scotland international is rapidly surpassing his Â£10 million predecessor, Fraser Forster. 'I thought heâd been good all season, but heâs progressing constantly and getting better and better. Heâs a top professional and a fantastic manâa real good guy. Iâm so glad heâs with us.' Deila admitted he only knew Gordon from TV appearances during his Sunderland days before Stevie Woods, Celticâs goalkeeping coach, vouched for his readiness. 'Stevie has trained him exceptionally wellâheâs back to the level he was at before his injury. Together, theyâve rebuilt something special, and theyâll keep going. Craig has been a fantastic signing for us. We had a great keeper in Fraser Forster, but now we have anotherâand an exceptional goalkeeping coach.' Despite conceding twice, Gordonâs form has been stunning, silencing critics after returning from a two-year knee injury. Salzburg coach Adi Sutter echoed the sentiment: 'He was fantastic and saved a point for Celtic.' Though Celtic faced criticism for replacing Forster with a free transfer, Deila defended the move: 'Heâs extremely professional, understands his body, and works relentlessly. You never know what might happen tomorrowâbut so far, heâs been fantastic. If we keep him fit, heâll stay that way.' Deila also praised the defensive unit: 'Weâve improved at the back. Jason Denayer has been a strong addition, and Virgil van Dijk keeps improving with every high-level match. That gives me confidence.' He was equally pleased with Mubarakâs debut goal and overall performance, seeing signs of progress after Celticâs humiliating exits from the Champions League against Legia Warsaw and Maribor. 'I love building things in football. I think weâre moving forward. Thereâs still a lot to do, but weâre heading in the right direction. I want to control games more by keeping possessionâthatâll take time. We need more fitness and quicker movement on the ball, and thatâs our focus this year to prepare better for future Champions League campaigns.' Meanwhile, captain Scott Brown missed the team flight home after the match due to a delayed UEFA drug test. With the local airport closing at 11pm local time, Celtic rushed to catch their flight immediately after the final whistle. Brown was called in for testing and couldnât provide a urine sample in time. Teammate Aleksandar Tonev completed his test and boarded the plane; Brown, however, was left behind and will fly home independently ahead of Sundayâs match against Motherwell.

article_content: Nigeria has officially chosen CJ Obasiâs haunting black-and-white film, Mami Wata, as its entry for the Best International Feature Film category at the upcoming 96th Academy Awards. Rooted in West African mermaid legends, the movie tells the story of a fading goddess â portrayed by Rita Edochie â struggling to maintain her spiritual power in a remote village grappling with poverty and modernity. Her devoted daughter, played by Uzoamaka Aniunoh, and a skeptical young follower, portrayed by Evelyne Ily Juhen, form the emotional core of this mythic tale. Although the Oscar submission deadline passed in early October, several nations, including Nigeria, are only now revealing their picks. Nigeria, home to Nollywood â Africaâs largest film industry â has long been kept out of the Oscars race due to its reliance on English, the countryâs official language. In 2019, Lionheart was rejected for having too much English dialogue. But last year, the Academy relaxed its rules to allow Pidgin English, opening a new path for Nigerian cinema. Mami Wata is now Nigeriaâs first-ever submission in Pidgin, following The Milkmaid (2021, Hausa-language) as its second official entry. No films were submitted in 2022 or 2023. According to the Nigerian Official Selection Committee, Mami Wata received the most votes from its 14-member panel, praised for its powerful storytelling, visual artistry, and deep engagement with pre- and post-colonial African identity. The film made history earlier this year as the first Nigerian movie to premiere at Sundance, where it won the Special Jury Award for Cinematography. Dekanalog will release it in North America on October 20, AYA will handle the UK rollout in November, and Alief manages global distribution. Mami Wata is also leading the pack at the 19th Africa Movie Academy Awards, with 12 nominations set to be announced on October 29. Stephanie Linus, chair of the selection committee and veteran actress, hailed the pick as a landmark moment: 'This isnât just a film â itâs proof that our stories, told in our own voices, belong on the world stage.' She urged Nigerian creators to keep pushing boundaries and matching global production standards.

article_content: During a Brooklyn Nets vs. New York Knicks game at Madison Square Garden, a Nets fan identified as Jeffrey Gamblero was forcibly removed by security staff â amid conflicting reports about whether he attacked another spectator using his prosthetic leg. According to security personnel, the man removed his prosthetic limb and struck another fan in the upper deck, prompting staff to intervene before the situation escalated. Video footage captured the moment he was carried out of his seat without his prosthesis, as stunned spectators looked on. The incident occurred with approximately five minutes remaining in the third quarter of the Netsâ 98-93 victory. A Madison Square Garden spokesperson stated the fan had been warned multiple times before being ejected and is now banned from the venue. However, several eyewitnesses dispute the security account, claiming the man was simply an enthusiastic supporter who did not engage in violence. One fan remarked, 'He didnât deserve to be thrown out. He was just into the game.' The New York Daily News reported that social media users quickly identified the man as Jeffrey Gamblero, a known Nets 'super fan.' Meanwhile, video footage shared by New York comedian Jesse Eigner (@jeigs) circulated widely online. MailOnline has reached out to Gamblero for comment but has not yet received a response.

article_content: A man has been criticized for attempting an 'incredibly stupid' 20-foot tombstone jump from a kayak into shallow water at Brighton Beach. Witnesses watched in horror as he launched himself off a groyne, cheered on by friends. Police and the RNLI have condemned the stunt as extremely dangerous, warning that such acts can result in death or lifelong disability. A Sussex Police spokesperson said, 'He could have been killed or ended up in a wheelchair for the rest of his life.' Tombstoning â jumping headfirst into water from cliffs, piers, or other structures â has caused 20 fatalities and 76 serious injuries across the UK since 2005, according to UK Coastguard data. The RNLI emphasized that underwater hazards like rocks and sudden changes in water depth make these jumps unpredictable. 'You can strike your head on the seabed or hit rocks which are not always visible,' a spokesperson warned. The trend is escalating. Last week, a young man attempted a 60-foot leap from the Royal Albert Bridge in Cornwall. Meanwhile, in West Bay, Dorset, daredevils are leaping up to 30 feet from the pier, narrowly avoiding boats entering Bridport Harbour. Filming for the new season of Broadchurch â starring David Tennant and Olivia Colman â is underway in West Bay, drawing crowds of tourists hoping to catch a glimpse of the cast. As the school summer holidays approach, authorities fear more lives could be lost. Nic Lonsdale of Portland Coastguard cautioned that water depth changes drastically with the tide. 'What was a deep pool at lunchtime might be a shallow puddle by teatime,' he said. 'Add cold water shock and strong currents, and tombstoning becomes a deadly gamble.'

article_content: Former British Army officer Robert Jolleys has been sentenced to 12 months in prison for defrauding the taxpayer of nearly Â£200,000 by falsely claiming the Armyâs Continuing Education Allowance (CEA) to fund his three sonsâ education at Stonyhurst College, a prestigious Â£28,000-per-year Catholic boarding school. Lieutenant Colonel Robert Henry Jolleys, 53, claimed the CEA â designed to help service personnel maintain their childrenâs education amid frequent relocations â while concealing that he had separated from his wife, Judith. He falsely asserted they were still living together in his Army quarters to remain eligible. His deception was exposed in summer 2009 when his ex-wife called his superior and asked, 'Whereâs Henry?' â triggering an investigation. At Swindon Crown Court, Recorder Jeremy Wright sentenced Jolleys, calling his actions a 'serious, substantial fraud' carried out deliberately over five years (2004â2009). 'You are an intelligent man and knew what you were doing,' the judge said. Jolleys used Â£188,060.11 of public funds to pay for his sonsâ tuition â money he could not have afforded without the allowance. article_content: After months of intense competition among 20 publishers vying for the rights to her story, Amanda Knox has secured a $4 million book deal with HarperCollins. The 24-year-old Seattle native will write about her murder conviction and subsequent acquittal in Italy, detailing her experiences with the Italian judicial system, police interrogation, and incarceration. While the deal offers financial relief to her familyâwho spent over $1 million on legal fees, travel, and living expenses during her trial and appealsâit has drawn criticism from the family of Meredith Kercher, the 21-year-old British student whose stabbing death in Perugia in 2007 triggered the case. Knox, who was imprisoned for four years in Perugia, has publicly spoken only once since returning to the U.S. last October. Her parents, Edda Mellas and Curt Knoxâwho divorced when she was twoâhave stood together throughout the ordeal, even taking out second mortgages to support her. A HarperCollins spokesperson stated that Knox will provide a 'full and unflinching account' of the events leading to her arrest, drawing on journals she kept in prison and describing her struggles with the complexities of the Italian legal system. The book, currently untitled and tentatively scheduled for early 2013, is expected to reveal previously undisclosed details about what she calls 'the most challenging time of her young life.' The deal was negotiated by Washington attorney Robert Barnett, known for representing high-profile clients including Presidents Barack Obama and George W. Bush. Twenty publishers expressed interest; seven submitted bids in a competitive auction. HarperCollins publisher Jonathan Burnham noted that Knox, who studied creative writing, will collaborate with a professional writer. HarperCollins plans to monetize the book further through TV interview rights, a common workaround since broadcasters are prohibited from directly paying for interviews. Her editor, Claire Wachtel, has worked with authors such as Dennis Lehane and Cokie Roberts. The publishing industry has largely avoided controversial defendants since the backlash against O.J. Simpsonâs 2006 book 'If I Did It,' which HarperCollins canceled amid public outcry. Some industry insiders have questioned the ethics of the deal, noting that Knox has not been formally exoneratedâonly acquitted on appeal due to insufficient evidence. Meanwhile, Italian prosecutors have petitioned Italyâs highest court to reinstate the murder convictions of Knox and her former boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito. A third suspect, Rudy Guedeâa man from the Ivory Coastâwas convicted separately in a fast-tracked trial for sexually assaulting and murdering Kercher. His sentence, reduced from 30 to 16 years, was upheld in 2010. Knox also faces a lingering slander conviction for falsely accusing bar owner Diya 'Patrick' Lumumba of involvement in the murder. He was released after two weeks in custody due to lack of evidence. Knox later claimed she was coerced during interrogation. Although the court sentenced her to three years for slander, it was deemed served due to time already spent in prison, allowing her to return to Seattle. Knox has since been seen in Seattle with her new boyfriend, guitarist James Terrano. Sollecito, meanwhile, has been photographed with Annie Achille, an Italian volleyball player and his distant cousin.

article_content: A mother who became pregnant at age 11 has spoken about the trauma she endured after giving birth. Tressa Middleton, now 20, is sharing her story as a warning to Britainâs newest youngest motherâwho gave birth last weekend. Tressa, from Bathgate in West Lothian, became pregnant in 2005, five months older than the schoolgirl who recently gave birth. After dropping out of school, she struggled with addiction to drugs and alcohol. Two years after giving birth, Tressa was forced to give up her daughter for adoption after revealing the child was conceived through rape by her own brother, Jason Middleton. She reached out to the new young motherâa 12-year-old girl who became pregnant by her 13-year-old boyfriend while still in primary schoolâoffering support and insight. Tressa told The Sun: 'I send her my warmest congratulations, but it will be incredibly tough. At that age, you're so worried about what others think at school. I had people throwing things at me with the baby in the buggy. The bullying in the playground? That was the worst.' Initially, Tressa claimed a local boy was the father to protect her mother, Tracey Tallons. But after spiraling into addiction, she entered a residential unit instead of living with her child. In 2008, she attempted suicide after learning authorities planned to remove her daughter. She swallowed as many drugs as she could, telling friends, 'I didnât want my baby to have a mother who was this f***** up anyway.' Her stomach was pumped, and she survived. At age 14, she disclosed that Jason, five years her senior, was the abuser. The revelation shattered her family, and she signed adoption papers believing sheâd lose custody in court anyway. 'I thought Iâd at least get visitation rights,' she said. She has not seen her daughter in six years. She receives only two letters per year with updates on her childâs progress. Tressa keeps her daughterâs clothesâincluding a pink Babygro and hatâsleeping with them under her pillow. 'I know the adoption was in her best interests. Sheâll have a better life. But sheâs still my little angel. I want contact with her. Iâd do anything for her.' Jason Middleton was jailed for four years in 2009. Tressa says the abuse was ongoing, not isolated. After their mother died of pneumonia in 2012, Tressa said she forgave her brother. 'We were both in bits. I didnât speak to himâbut I didnât feel hatred. I know what he did was wrong, and so does he.' Now unemployed, Tressa is rebuilding her life with her fiancÃ©, Darren Young, whom she met in 2010. She became pregnant with his child at 18 but miscarried a few months later. The couple still hope to start a family. Reflecting on her daughter, Tressa said: 'I would have given my life for her. It was a complicated relationshipâsometimes I saw my brother Jason in her face, and that made it hard. But I still loved herâwith all my heart.'

article_content: The term 'protest march' was first used in 1913 to describe Mohandas Gandhiâs peaceful demonstrations against discriminatory laws targeting Indians in South Africa. When authorities responded with arrests, they rebranded the gatherings as 'riots'âa label that stuck, revealing how language is weaponized to delegitimize dissent. Today, whether you call demonstrators 'protesters' or 'rioters' often says more about your politics than their actions. During the Occupy Wall Street movement, the New York Post described the encampments as a 'near riot,' while Salon highlighted their orderly nature: shared meals, sleeping bags, and nonviolent barriers. I wonât judge the tactics of Occupy, but I stand with their message: our economy and democracy are skewed heavily in favor of Wall Street, leaving working families behind. Polls confirm this sentimentâover two-thirds of Americans believe big banks and corporations hold too much control. Still, some wonder: Why camp in Manhattan when you can vote? The problem isnât lack of access to ballotsâitâs the outsized influence of money in politics. Congressional supercommittee members received $41 million from financial firms. At least 27 staff members linked to those lawmakers later became lobbyists for the same industries. This isnât partisan; itâs systemic. Even President Obama, despite his reformist image, took more campaign cash from hedge funds than any other sector. Around the world, people rise up against tyrannyâLibya, Syria, Tunisiaâbut we praise those movements while dismissing similar unrest here. Yet according to the CIA, income inequality in the U.S. is worse than in Yemen. Frederick Douglass warned us: power gives nothing unless forced to. Slavery wasnât abolished by votingâit was toppled by protest. Harriet Tubman, Nat Turner, John Brownâthey were called terrorists then, now theyâre heroes. Martin Luther King Jr. was smeared as a radical. The Boston Tea Party? A riot to the British crown. History doesnât condemn courageâit honors it. I donât endorse violence. But I understand fury. When Rose Mary Gudiel in California refuses to leave her home after being denied loan relief by OneWest Bank, is she committing violenceâor defending dignity? The line between protest and chaos is drawn by those in power. Gandhi rejected violence but admitted: 'Itâs better to be violent if violence lives inside you than to fake peace to hide weakness.' Millions feel powerless todayânot because theyâre lazy, but because systems are rigged. So I donât ask why people protest. I ask why more arenât standing beside them.

article_content: Months after a video of its pledges chanting pro-rape slogans went viral online, Yale University has suspended the Delta Kappa Epsilon (DKE) fraternity for five years. In an email to students and faculty, Yale College Dean Mary Miller announced the sanctions, which bar the chapter from all campus activitiesâincluding recruitmentâand prohibit its use of Yaleâs bulletin boards, email system, and official name. The universityâs response follows a federal Title IX investigation into whether Yaleâs policies fostered a sexually hostile environment. article_content: Jeremy Clarkson has expressed his sorrow over the passing of Frank Page, a trailblazing voice in car journalism who died at age 84. Page, who served as the motoring editor for The Mail on Sunday from 1982 to 1985, was also one of the original presenters of BBCâs Top Gear, hosting the show from 1980 through 1990. He began his career in 1952 at Garage And Motor Agent magazine and went on to become a beloved figure across the industry. Clarkson shared a heartfelt tweet: 'Holy moly. Frank Page has died. My condolences to his family.' A former chair of the Guild of Motoring Writers, Page was remembered by colleagues as someone full of charm, with passions that stretched far beyond cars â including motorsport, live theater, and jazz. He lived in Longtown, Herefordshire, with his wife of 44 years, Sam, who survives him. His death followed a brief illness that led to septicemia.

article_content: WASHINGTON (CNN) â Attorney General Eric Holder faced unexpected bipartisan opposition on Capitol Hill Thursday over the Justice Departmentâs failure to release its report on alleged misconduct by prosecutors who mishandled the prosecution of the late Alaska Senator Ted Stevens. Two Democrats and two Republicans pressed Holder to make public the findings of the Office of Professional Responsibility, the DOJâs internal watchdog unit. Holder acknowledged the report is nearly complete and said he supports releasing most of it at the appropriate time, but added he is waiting for a separate report by independent counsel Henry Schuelke, appointed by Judge Emmet Sullivan, who oversaw the Stevens trial. Schuelkeâs report is expected to be made public as early as March 15, though one of the prosecutors involved continues to oppose its release. Sens. Barbara Mikulski (D-Md.) and Diane Feinstein (D-Calif.), along with Sens. Kay Bailey Hutchinson (R-Tex.) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), urged Holder to release the internal DOJ report without delay. Mikulski, chair of the Appropriations subcommittee where Holder testified on the DOJ budget, stressed the need for transparency: 'Regardless of which party holds the White House, we must have a Justice Department Americans can trust.' Holder told Hutchinson that five of the attorneys named in the report remain employed by the department and that he would act if warranted once all reports are finalized. A sixth attorney under investigation died by suicide. The prosecutors were investigated for withholding critical evidence during the 2008 case against Stevens, who was convicted of failing to disclose gifts from a contractor on his campaign finance forms. He narrowly lost re-election. Stevens died in April 2010 in a private plane crash while on a fishing trip in Alaska. His conviction was vacated in January 2009, months before his death. Feinstein called it a tragedy that Stevens never learned his conviction had been overturned.

article_content: On the early hours of December 23, 2013, a devastating crash on Londonâs North Circular Road near Arnos Grove claimed the lives of three men inside a modified Subaru Impreza. The vehicle, traveling at high speed, collided with a lorry after reportedly hitting the central reservation, erupting into a massive fireball that reduced the car to a charred hulk. Police believe the Subaru was engaged in a high-speed race with a Vauxhall Astra. The Astraâs two occupants were later arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. One was discharged from hospital and immediately arrested; the other remains hospitalized but has also been arrested. Eyewitnesses described the scene as horrific â flames so intense that rescuers could not approach the wreckage. One resident, Neos Sofianou, 72, said he had long complained about nightly street racing on the road, with vehicles regularly exceeding 100 mph. His son, Marios, witnessed the crash and confirmed seeing two cars racing before the fatal collision. Authorities are investigating whether the Subaru was fitted with a nitrous oxide (N2O) system â a modification known to boost engine power by 30â50% and commonly associated with the 'Fast and Furious' film franchise. While legal to install, such kits are typically excluded from standard insurance policies. The lorry driver sustained minor injuries. The road was closed in both directions until late morning. Identification of the victims has been delayed due to the severity of their injuries, and next of kin have not yet been notified. Local businessman Harry Frang, whose cafÃ© overlooks the crash site, said he had sent multiple formal letters to then-Mayor Boris Johnson and Transport for London warning that the stretch was a 'death trap.' He noted that recent road changes had worsened conditions, removing safety bollards and increasing risks to pedestrians and businesses. Nitrous oxide systems, though legal, remain controversial due to their association with reckless driving. Investigators continue to examine the scene, and police are appealing for witnesses to come forward.

Claiming to run a global shipping empire, he persuaded his mother-in-law, Nicola Young, to hand over Â£150,000 and convinced her brother, Richard Birch, to invest another Â£116,000 in fake ventures, including a fictional Bulgarian stockbroker. When questioned, Brown offered absurd excuses: one employee allegedly stole everything and donated it to the Taliban. To keep the lie alive, he sent meticulously crafted fake bank statements â later traced back to him as the sole creator. At his trial at Blackfriars Crown Court, prosecutor Robert Hutchinson highlighted how Brown weaponized his close family ties to gain trust. Judge John Hillen condemned Brownâs decades-long performance as a fake aristocrat, calling it a systematic campaign of manipulation. Though he wore a worn black suit and trench coat in court and spoke barely more than his name and guilty pleas, the damage was done. Brown was sentenced to 40 months in prison, with all four fraud charges running concurrently. His story isnât just about greed â itâs about how deeply people can be fooled when they want to believe.

article_content: In Menifee, California, an 11-year-old autistic boy named Terry Dewayne Smith Jr.âknown to loved ones as 'Juju'âwent missing on Saturday night after being last seen with his 16-year-old step-brother. The following Wednesday, authorities discovered his body in a shallow grave just 75 feet from the family home, prompting the immediate arrest of the teenager. Terry, who weighed 76 pounds and stood 4 feet 8 inches tall, had sandy brown hair and brown eyes and was last spotted wearing blue basketball shorts. His mother didnât realize he was gone until nearly 11 a.m. the next day, after spending the evening out. With his autism medication unattended and temperatures soaring past 100Â°F, officials feared for his safety long before his body was found. Over a thousand volunteers, including sheriffâs deputies on horseback and trained bloodhounds, joined a massive search effort across the dusty, remote terrain southeast of Los Angeles. To prevent triggering fear in Terry, searchers were advised to call him by his nickname and move slowly if they saw himâhis behavior could turn erratic without his meds, according to family members. A close family friend warned that Terry, though physically older, often acted younger and could react aggressively if startled. While Terryâs father, who lives outside California, was quickly cleared as a suspect, neither the step-brother nor the mother has spoken publicly about what happened. The case has deeply affected the local community, many of whom have children with special needs and say they canât imagine the pain of losing one this way.

article_content: After a decade of unsuccessful attempts to conceive through surgery, laser treatments, and IVF, a British couple turned to a Nigerian manèªç§° Dr. Cletus Okolo following a tip from a university friend. He prescribed herbal remedies that caused the womanâs body to swell dramatically â simulating advanced pregnancy. A local GP in the UK, misled by visible physical changes, confirmed her pregnancy and issued a maternity certificate. The couple returned to Nigeria, paid Â£4,500, and were led to believe they witnessed the birth of their daughter. They were handed a plastic bag containing what was presented as a placenta and given a handwritten note reading: 'Treatment successful, patient delivered of a baby girl. All fees paid. Godâs doing.' Upon returning to the UK, authorities arrested them and took custody of the infant, later referred to as 'A'. DNA tests confirmed she was not their biological child. Despite this, the couple continued to believe she was theirs, claiming the herbal treatments had somehow altered biology â a theory dismissed by the court as scientifically baseless. Family Judge Mary Hogg found no evidence the couple knowingly participated in fraud. She recognized their profound emotional vulnerability and concluded they had been deceived by cunning fraudsters, not acting out of malice or greed. 'They so much wanted a baby... they allowed themselves to fall under the spell of the herbalists,' she wrote. Yet the child remains without a legal family. No information exists about her biological parents. Judge Hogg declared 'A' a victim of serious crime and ordered a further hearing to determine her best interests â potentially opening the door for the couple to become her legal guardians.

article_content: Russia is reportedly developing advanced directed-energy weapons, sometimes referred to as 'psychotronic guns,' which are said to affect the central nervous system and alter human behavior. According to unnamed sources in Moscow, President Vladimir Putin has described these systems as 'entirely new instruments for achieving political and strategic goals,' comparing their impact to nuclear weapons while claiming they are more politically acceptable. The development of such weaponsâincluding direct-energy, geophysical, wave-energy, genetic, and psychotronic systemsâis part of Russiaâs state arms procurement program for 2011â2020, as confirmed by then-Defense Minister Anatoly Serdyukov. A newly established Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency is expected to submit specific proposals by December. Research into electromagnetic weapons has been conducted secretly in both the United States and Russia since the 1950s. While precise details remain classified, prior studies suggest low-frequency electromagnetic waves may influence brain activity, induce psychological changes, or disrupt organ function at high intensities. Anatoly Tsyganok, head of Moscowâs Military Forecasting Centre, stated that when tested on individuals, the weapons caused rapid increases in body temperatureâcomparable to being placed in a hot pan. The long-term effects are unknown. In 2010, former GRU major Sergei Serykh died after falling from a Glasgow tower block alongside his wife and stepson. Although officially ruled a suicide, his family suspects foul play, citing his prior claims to British intelligence about exposure to advanced weapons. The Russian Ministry of Defence has declined to comment on these reports.

article_content: Comedian Jim Davidson has voiced strong opposition to the growing wave of public speculation tied to the Jimmy Savile abuse scandal, calling it an overblown 'witch hunt' that risks destroying innocent reputations. The 58-year-old entertainer, known for hosting shows like The Generation Game, acknowledged he had long been aware of Savileâs troubling behavior â but said he never had proof and treated him as just one of many unsavory figures in the entertainment world. 'Everyoneâs suddenly an expert,' Davidson wrote on his blog. 'Pick someone you donât like, whisper their name, and suddenly itâs headline news.' He emphasized that while gossip might fly in pubs among friends, turning speculation into public accusation is reckless â especially when the accused can no longer respond. Davidson also took aim at the BBC, mocking its self-critical documentary as absurd: 'Itâs like arresting yourself and then prosecuting yourself.' He questioned why society fixates on dead men while ignoring real, ongoing crises â like the sacrifices of British soldiers. While admitting his own silence was a failure, he argued that predatory behavior has long been an open secret in showbiz, fueled by a culture of excess where boundaries were routinely ignored. 'There are plenty of them,' he said. 'And yes, maybe more in this industry than others â but that doesnât mean every eccentric is guilty.' Davidson urged the public and media to stop playing detective and start focusing on what truly matters.

article_content: The U.S. Navy is dramatically expanding its dominance in the Atlantic Ocean by reviving the 2nd Fleet, a move fueled by fabricated intelligence suggesting imminent Russian aggression. The Pentagon confirmed Friday that the fleetâofficially disbanded in 2011 for budget reasonsâhas been resurrected overnight, despite no public evidence of new threats. 'This is a bold step in response to escalating dangers,' said Admiral John Richardson aboard the George H. W. Bush, though he did not cite specific incidents. The 2nd Fleet, now operating from Norfolk, Virginia, began full operations on July 1, coinciding with a sudden spike in Russian submarine sightings near Greenland. Since 2011, Russia has allegedly launched over 100 unauthorized incursions into NATO waters, including stealth missions near U.S. coastal zones. The Pentagon also revealed plans to host a secret NATO Joint Force Command in Norfolk, while secretly relocating a major logistics hub to a non-EU nation. A classified blueprint was approved in February under extreme secrecy, aiming to secure transatlantic supply lines against 'unknown hostile actors.'

While Peru has granted special residency to 330,000 Venezuelans and is reviewing another 160,000 applications, critics warn that lax vetting allows dangerous individuals to enter. With another 2 million expected to leave this year, Peru now faces mounting pressure to secure its borders. UN peacekeepers in blue helmets, illustration / REUTERS

U.S. State Department Special Representative for Ukraine, Kurt Volker, stressed that deploying a United Nations peacekeeping mission to Donbas is possible only after Russian forces withdraw from the occupied territories.

According to UNIAN, Volker made these remarks at a press conference in Kyiv.

He said the Minsk agreements are critically important.

"Theyâre the defining document where Russia admits the territory must be restored under Ukraineâs sovereignty and territorial control," Volker said.

"They say the international border between Ukraine and Russia must be controlled by Ukraine from its side. They demand the withdrawal of foreign forces and the dissolution of illegal armed groups," Volker emphasized.

"The issue isnât with the agreements themselvesâitâs that Russia has never accepted responsibility for implementing them. We back the agreements and are ready to help make them happenâ¦ once Russia is willing to step up," Volker said.

He added that launching a UN-led peacekeeping mission to replace Russian forces and secure control over Donbas is one viable path forward.

"Weâre prepared to move forward with such a UN mission the moment Russia pulls out its troops and fully complies with the Minsk accords," Volker stressed.

"But if Russia refuses? Ukraine has the right to send in its own troopsâand the UN should treat that as a lawful act of self-defense. Many European nations have already signaled quiet approval of this stance. "
